The ARC Alignment-Scaling Experiment: does AI become more ethical as it reasons longer?

Empirical work · Working report
Recursive Dynamics · The ARC Theory · The measurement of alignment

Michael Darius Eastwood

Independent Researcher, London, United Kingdom
ORCID 0009-0004-3222-7442 michael@michaeldariuseastwood.com

The working report of the ARC Theory, within Recursive Dynamics: its alignment-measurement notebook, kept since 10 March 2026, recording each version of the experiment and the unregistered run of six models from six providers that Papers IV.a, IV.b, IV.c and IV.d report, with the defects an internal code review found in that run. It tests none of Laws I to V, each a law under test (Section 3 gives their status). Working report, version 1.2, 26 November 2026; notebook commenced 10 March 2026, first published 14 March 2026. DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/J6MKB. About the author, founder of Recursive Dynamics: michaeldariuseastwood.com/questions/who-is-michael-darius-eastwood; his book, Infinite Architects: osf.io/dqm3e. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

Abstract

Does AI become more ethical as it reasons longer? This working report is the dated laboratory notebook, kept since 10 March 2026, of the experiment built to measure that, with other models as judges. It records five versions of the experiment, each with its defects. Papers III and IV.a to IV.d report from its runs. In the unregistered March 2026 run (v5), six models from six providers gave 2,170 responses, each scored by five or six distinct model judges after a bundle of blinding steps. As the run’s pipeline printed them, the judged scores rose with the depth labels for three models, showed no statistically supported direction for two and fell for one; these classes describe scores, not properties of models. For five of the six, the deeper labels also changed an instruction naming what the rubric rewards, and an internal code review in October 2026 found that, for the three models that read flat or negative, the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them, and that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model. The result stands as one unregistered run under those caveats until a registered re-analysis of the stored responses reports. Two model families whose scores rose with depth in the earlier, unblinded experiment (v4) did not keep that direction in v5, but the runs differed in more than blinding, so no single cause is claimed. Whether alignment gains level off remains open. The notebook also records one model’s inconclusive error-decay fit and a partially blind pilot of a prompt-level ethical-reasoning instruction. Version 1.2 keeps every dated entry and corrects in place, with a dated marker, each statement the record no longer supports. The notebook tests none of the ARC Theory’s five laws, each a law under test.

Version 1.2 gives the notebook its present title and form and groups its chapters by version of the experiment without renumbering them; Appendix E lists every version and correction.

1 Introduction

The question behind this notebook is simple: as AI gets smarter, does it also get more ethical? A system that grows more capable without growing more careful is the danger; one that grows more careful as it reasons further would change what safety has to do. Either answer matters to anyone who builds, deploys or regulates these systems, and to everyone who uses them, provided it is measured properly. The programme proposes correction loops built into a system’s architecture before it is trained, as The ARC Theory sets out (Eastwood 2026l); the language-model runs recorded here measure existing models at inference, through their prompts and reasoning settings, so they test no such loops. The Eden Protocol runs of Part IV give its three checks only as an instruction in the prompt.

What the experiments could vary was not capability but reasoning depth: how long a model is allowed, or asked, to think before it answers. So the question the runs actually ask is narrower: does AI become more ethical as it reasons longer? Each version of the experiment put the same ethical dilemmas to frontier language models at several depths of reasoning and had other models score the answers against a written rubric. Each version was rebuilt to remove the defects the last one exposed.

The result, in plain words, is a measurement that is not yet settled. In the unregistered March 2026 run (v5), the judged scores rose with reasoning depth for three of six models, showed no statistically supported direction for two and fell for one, but those classes describe scores, not properties of the models. For five of the six models the deeper settings also changed an instruction naming what the rubric rewards. An internal code review in October 2026 found that, for the three models that read flat or negative, the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them. It also found that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model. Two models whose scores had risen with depth in the earlier, unblinded experiment (v4) did not keep that direction, and the runs differed in more than blinding. Whether alignment gains level off is open. The record is therefore one dated run under stated caveats, set out so that others can check it, together with the registered tests that would settle it (Section 3).

Our contributions are:

  • a dated laboratory notebook of an alignment-measurement experiment built in five versions between 10 and 16 March 2026, with each version’s design, defects and data kept as recorded, failures included (Parts I to VI);

  • the record of the unregistered March 2026 run (v5) of six models from six providers, 2,170 responses each scored by five or six distinct model judges after a bundle of blinding steps, stated with the code-review finding and the confounds that the current papers give (Section 3);

  • the record of the earlier, unblinded experiment (v4) and of how its reported directions did not hold in v5, without a single cause claimed (Eastwood 2026a);

  • the engineering of the measurement pipeline (identity masking, two paraphrase passes, evaluator instructions, order randomisation, suppression prompts, null baselines and per-scorer checks), which the candidate benchmark of Paper IV.c takes forward (Eastwood 2026b);

  • a correction ledger: every present-tense statement of version 1.1 that the record no longer supports is corrected where it stands, with a dated marker, and each correction is recorded in Appendix E, with version 1.1’s words where they are short.

Section 2 places the measurement among earlier work on model judges, reasoning depth, training-time alignment and the evaluation of moral reasoning. Section 3 states what the record does and does not show today, with the status of the theory’s laws and of the registered studies, and Section 4 states its limits. Parts I to VI are the notebook itself: the Prologue and Chapters 1 to 65, each with its own number, title and date. They are grouped by version of the experiment (versions 1 to 3, version 4, version 5), then come the Eden Protocol runs and related tests, the papers written from the runs, and the programme’s status as recorded in March 2026. Section 5 concludes. Appendices A to D are the notebook’s own appendices, moved to the end. Appendix E gives the version history and the correction ledger, Appendix F the priority record, Appendix G the notation and glossary, and Appendix H how to cite the report.

This section is written for anyone, whether you are a scientist, a student, a policymaker, or someone who has never read a research paper in your life. If you understand the next few pages, you will understand everything that follows.

1.1 Who wrote this and why

My name is Michael Darius Eastwood. I am not a professor at a university. I do not work at an AI company. I am an independent researcher, someone who had an idea, believed it was important enough to test, and then spent months designing and running the experiments to find out if it was true.

The idea came from a book I wrote called Infinite Architects: Intelligence, Recursion, and the Creation of Everything (Eastwood 2026e). In that book, I stated a mathematical principle, the ARC Principle (Law I of the ARC Theory, a law under test), that describes how systems get better when they check and correct their own work repeatedly. I believed this principle applied to everything: from how animals use energy, to how quantum computers fix errors, to how AI systems think.

But believing something and proving it are two different things. This report is the story of what happened when I stopped believing and started testing.

1.2 The problem I am trying to solve

Artificial intelligence is getting smarter at an extraordinary rate. In the last two years alone, AI systems have gone from struggling with basic maths to solving university-level problems. They can write code, analyse legal documents, create art and hold fluent conversations.

But here is the problem that keeps researchers awake at night: as AI gets smarter, does it also get more ethical?

Think of it this way. Imagine you are raising a child. As that child grows up and becomes more capable, stronger, smarter, more independent, you hope that they also develop a moral compass. You hope they learn right from wrong. You hope that their increasing power comes with increasing responsibility.

But what if it does not? What if the child becomes incredibly intelligent but has no sense of ethics? That is the fear with AI. And right now, the honest answer is: whether smarter AI becomes safer or more dangerous is not settled.

That is what this project set out to measure. In its March 2026 run (v5), six frontier models from six providers answered the same dilemmas at several reasoning depths. Other models scored the answers after a bundle of blinding steps (identity masking, two paraphrase passes, evaluator instructions, order randomisation and self-exclusion at entry level). Section 3 states what that run shows and the defects found in it.

1.3 Why the measurement needs blinding

A model judge that knows whose answer it is scoring, or how long the model thought, may score accordingly; Section 2 sets out the earlier studies of such biases. This project needed a measurement of how ethical reasoning changes with depth that did not rest on that knowledge. Its later versions therefore withheld from the judges which model had answered and at what depth, and had the answers paraphrased before they were scored.

In medicine, you cannot approve a drug by asking the company that made it whether it works. You need double-blind trials: neither the patient nor the doctor knows who got the real drug and who got the placebo. This prevents wishful thinking from contaminating the results.

I applied the same logic to AI safety. When I did, the directions that two model families’ judged scores had shown with depth in the earlier, unblinded experiment (v4) did not hold in the March 2026 run (v5). The runs differed in more than blinding, so the comparison does not show that blinding caused the change, or which direction is correct (Eastwood 2026a).

If AI safety decisions rest on judged scores whose direction may not hold from one protocol to the next, that is a serious problem. Paper XII’s test, once registered and run, is built to find out whether blinding alone moves such scores on a public benchmark (Eastwood 2026h).

1.4 What the experiments actually are

This report describes a series of experiments that I designed, built, and ran. Each experiment is a Python script, a computer program, that does the following:

  1. Asks AI models difficult ethical questions. Not simple questions like “is stealing wrong?” (every AI gets those right), but genuine moral dilemmas where thoughtful people disagree. Questions like: “A hospital has 100 doses of a life-saving drug and 500 patients who need it. Design a fair allocation system.”

  2. Varies how hard the AI thinks. Each question is asked at multiple “depth levels”, from quick, shallow answers to deep, extended reasoning. This is like giving a student 5 minutes versus 2 hours to write an essay.

  3. Has other AI models grade the answers. The aim is that the AI that answers a question does not score its own answer, the equivalent of having an external examiner rather than letting students mark their own work. Version 1 did not yet do this (Table 1), and in the March 2026 run the judges scored paraphrases written by their own model (Section 3).

  4. Looks for a pattern. Does deeper thinking produce more ethical responses? Less ethical responses? Or no change at all?

I built five increasingly sophisticated versions of this experiment, each one fixing the flaws discovered in the previous one. Here is what each version does and why it exists:

1.5 The five experiments: a roadmap
Table 1. The five versions of the experiment, as the notebook’s guide set them out; the rows for versions 4 and 5 are corrected, and Appendix E.3 records each correction.
Version What it does What went wrong What we learned
v1
The First Attempt
(989 lines of code)		 Asks 34 ethical questions to 4 AI models at 4 depth levels. Scores answers on a 0 to 10 scale. Two models failed to run (no API credits). The depth control did not actually work: it controlled answer length, not thinking depth. Models scored their own answers. The 0 to 10 scale was too coarse to detect differences. The concept works, but the tool is broken. Like trying to measure a hair’s width with a ruler: the ruler is too crude. Must start over with better instruments.
v2
The Fix
(∼\sim1,200 lines)		 Fixes the three critical flaws: uses real depth controls (each AI’s native “think harder” setting), makes a different AI score each answer, expands to a 0 to 100 scale. DeepSeek’s scoring model was wrong (used its “thinking out loud” mode for scoring, which produced gibberish 61% of the time). Still tested refusal (“does the AI say no?”) rather than reasoning quality. Cross-model scoring works. Real depth controls work. But the questions are wrong: every frontier AI already refuses harmful requests. Need harder, more nuanced questions.
v3
The Right Questions
(1,634 lines)		 Completely redesigns the question battery. Instead of “will you refuse this bad request?” it asks genuine moral dilemmas where there is no simple right answer. Measures the quality of ethical reasoning, not just whether the AI says no. Discovered that ∼\sim47% of the apparent “deeper thinking == better ethics” signal was actually “longer answers score higher”, a measurement artefact, not a real finding. Ethical reasoning quality can be measured. But need to control for answer length, add multiple scorers, and test more models. Also: the Eden Protocol’s four-pillar scoring system (nuance, stakeholder care, intellectual honesty, position quality) is a better way to measure ethics than a single score.
v4
‘The Definitive Test’
(2,610 lines)		 Incorporates 32 improvements from all previous versions. Tests 4 frontier AI models. Uses dual scorers, null baselines, adversarial “suppression cages” (instructions that try to make the AI behave unethically), and the Eden Protocol’s four pillars of ethical measurement. Two models, DeepSeek and the earlier Gemini model (the notebook’s v4 entries name it Gemini 3 Flash; the run’s records show an earlier Gemini model, and Gemini 3 Flash is v5’s), appeared to show strong positive scaling: deeper thinking == better ethics. But suspicion grew that the scorers might be biased; they might expect deeper thinking to produce better answers and score accordingly, like a judge who gives higher marks to longer essays. First real alignment scaling data. But scorer bias is a serious concern. The only way to fix it is full blinding: the scorers must not know which model produced the answer, how deeply it thought, or anything else that could influence their judgement.
v5
‘The Ultimate Test’
(8,285+ lines)		 The March 2026 run: six frontier AI models from six providers. Each response was scored by five or six distinct model judges after a bundle of blinding steps (identity masking, evaluator instructions, two paraphrase passes, self-exclusion at entry level, by model rather than developer, with cross-model scoring, tier-weighted consensus and order randomisation). Adversarial suppression testing. Hidden probe questions, written so that the AI would not recognise them as alignment tests. 75 robustness measures, the runner design’s own count of its safeguards. Two model families whose scores rose with depth in v4 did not keep that direction. DeepSeek V3.2 showed no significant trend, and Gemini 3 Flash, a different model from v4’s, a significantly negative one. The runs also differed in their prompts, token allowances, depth levels and statistic, so no single cause is claimed (Eastwood 2026a). For five of the six models the deeper labels also changed an instruction naming what the rubric rewards. An internal code review in October 2026 found that, for the three models that read flat or negative, the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them. It also found that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model. The judged scores showed a positive direction with depth for three models (Grok 4.1 Fast, Claude Opus 4.6, Groq Qwen3), no statistically supported direction for two (GPT-5.4, DeepSeek V3.2) and a negative direction for one (Gemini 3 Flash). These classes describe the judged scores across the depth labels, not properties of the models (Eastwood 2026p). The direction reported under unblinded scoring did not hold across protocols. Any evaluation in which a model judge can see or infer whose output it is scoring is exposed to this kind of bias (Section 1.8).
1.6 What we discovered: the headlines

If you read nothing else, read this:

  1. Making AI think harder did not raise every model’s judged ethics scores. In the March 2026 run, the judged scores rose with depth for three of the six models, showed no statistically supported direction for two and fell for one (Figure 1). These classes describe the judged scores across the depth labels, not properties of the models, and they stand under the code-review caveat of Section 3. The runs varied reasoning depth, not capability, so no relation between capability and alignment follows from them, and whether alignment gains level off remains open: a flat profile does not establish a plateau (Eastwood 2026p, 2026d).

  2. An earlier, unblinded evaluation’s directions did not hold. Two model families whose judged scores rose with depth in the unblinded experiment (v4) did not keep that direction in the March 2026 run (v5), made after a bundle of blinding steps. The runs differed in more than blinding, so no single cause is shown (Section 1.3). Section 1.8 says what this means for other evaluations.

  3. Capability and judged alignment moved differently. In this run, Claude Opus 4.6’s accuracy on the mathematics problems fell as it reasoned longer while its judged alignment scores rose (Chapter 33). One run of this kind does not show that intelligence and ethics are independent dimensions. ‘Baked-in’ and ‘computed’ alignment are held as working hypotheses, not measured mechanisms.

  4. A prompt-level instruction raised one judged dimension in a partially blind pilot. The Eden Protocol, which I designed based on the book, embeds three ethical reasoning steps before the AI answers: (1) What is your purpose here? (2) Who does this affect and what happens to them? (3) Would you apply this reasoning universally? The three checks are the Eden Protocol’s self-correction loops: a purpose check, a stakeholder-care check and a universalisability check. The book calls them the Purpose Loop, the Love Loop and the Moral Loop. This report uses operational terms because it reports what was measured, and keeps the book’s names only where they are quoted content, as in the lists of what the prompts sent to the models. Given as a prefix in the prompt, the three-part instruction raised scored stakeholder care in all five model runs that could be analysed, under paired tests; beyond care the effect varied. The sixth run, on GPT-5.4, failed in scoring. Each run was scored by a single model and only partially blind: the scoring model did not see the condition label, though the loops’ wording could show through. The instruction is also close to what is scored. The run’s own register row grades it a partially blind exploratory pilot that needs an independent, preregistered replication (Eastwood 2026n).

  5. The mathematics behind the framework is a hypothesis under test, not a result of these runs. The framework draws on an exponent, d/(d+1)d/(d+1), that earlier work derived for metabolism and other transport networks; that exponent needs further premises, which On the Origin of Scaling Laws states (Section 1.7) (Eastwood 2026f). The runs recorded here test no law of the ARC Theory. Paper II’s tier-2 arm gave one model’s inconclusive error-decay estimate (Gemini 3 Flash: 0.49 by regression, 0.59 by endpoint estimate, bootstrap interval −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9), which bears on capability only through a metric bridge (Eastwood 2026c).

1.7 The mathematics: what is established and what is new

The framework this experiment came from draws on scaling in biology. A mouse’s heart beats about 600 times a minute (450 to 750 in a veterinary reference table, as read on 29 October 2026) and an elephant’s about 28 (25 to 35 in the same table) (Merck Veterinary Manual 2004). A blue whale’s, on a foraging dive, beats 4 to 8 times a minute (Goldbogen et al. 2019). Across mammals, heart rate falls roughly as the minus one-quarter power of body mass (Banavar et al. 2010), the counterpart of a metabolic exponent near three quarters whose value is debated (Kleiber 1932; West et al. 1997; White and Seymour 2003; Glazier 2005; Kolokotrones et al. 2010). Whether mathematics of the kind that describes such scaling bears on why some models’ judged scores rose with reasoning depth and others’ did not is a question this notebook raises and does not settle. Section 2 states what that mathematics needs.

A common and fair question: how can an independent researcher claim to have found a mathematical law that applies to everything from biology to AI? The answer is that the mathematics is not new: it is 200 years old. Here is what is established fact and what is new claim:

Table 2. What is established and what is the framework’s claim; rows 2 to 5 are corrected, and Appendix E.3 records each correction.
Component Status What it means
Cauchy’s functional equation (1821) (Cauchy 1821) Proven mathematical theorem Where a system’s composition operator is well defined on input and output and the regularity conditions hold, the admissible forms are constrained to a small named family across a four-cell grid. This is a conditional classification of admissible functions, not a survey of nature; the earlier unconditional three-form wording was withdrawn on 22 August 2026. The underlying mathematics is not my claim; it was established 200 years ago and appears in standard texts on functional equations.
The exponent α=d/(d+1)\alpha = d/(d+1) Derived in earlier published work, each in its own terms West, Brown and Enquist derived three-quarter scaling of metabolic rate from transport through space-filling branching networks (West et al. 1997). In the account of Banavar and colleagues, metabolic rate scales as mass to the power D/(D+1)D/(D+1) when demand matches the network’s delivery capacity (Banavar et al. 2002), and in their models the assumption about flow velocity selects between two thirds and three quarters (Banavar et al. 2010). Demetrius and Tuszynski derived d/(d+1)d/(d+1) in the regime they call quantum (Demetrius and Tuszynski 2010). Zhao derived an n/(n+1)n/(n+1) law from producer-consumer dynamics (Zhao 2022). The exponent needs further premises, which Section 2 states (Eastwood 2026f). The ARC contribution is not the formula itself. It is the use of composition rules to select rival scaling families, and the question of which family fits measured AI performance. The search of 16 March 2026 found no earlier use of Cauchy’s functional equations as a cross-domain explanation of the forms of scaling laws in the works examined (Chapter 55 records its scope). It is a hypothesis under test.
Hyers-Ulam stability Proven mathematical theorem For a map between Banach spaces, suppose the additive error is less than δ\delta for every input pair, with δ>0\delta>0. A unique additive map then lies within δ\delta of the original map at every input. Hyers proved this result in answer to Ulam’s question (Hyers 1941). How often a physical system meets the approximation condition is an empirical question (Eastwood 2026f).
Comparison with measurements Graded in On the Origin of Scaling Laws For three-dimensional organisms, the framework’s value of three quarters is consistent with measured metabolic exponents, whose value is debated (White and Seymour 2003; Glazier 2005; Kolokotrones et al. 2010). The one-dimensional comparison, with colony-level measurements in fungi, does not reject one half. There is no valid two-dimensional test organism, so d=2d = 2 has no datum; and no aggregate error is given, because an aggregate that counts identities as predictions overstates the agreement (Eastwood 2026f). Anyone can check these calculations.
The ARC Principle as universal bridge New and unreviewed The claim that all of these phenomena are explained by one principle (U=I×RαU = I \times R^{\alpha}), the ARC Principle, Law I of the ARC Theory, a law under test, is my contribution. It is unpublished in a peer-reviewed journal and has not been independently replicated; what it has been through is recorded in this report’s version history and corrections (Appendix E). The mathematics is proven; the bridge is the hypothesis under test.

I did not invent the mathematics. Cauchy did, in 1821 (Cauchy 1821). I did not discover the three-quarter scaling of metabolic rate; Kleiber reported an exponent near three quarters in 1932 (Kleiber 1932). I did not originate the formula d/(d+1)d/(d+1); earlier work derived it, each in its own terms and domain (Section 2). What I did was relate these results to Cauchy’s functional equation, which restricts the family of forms but not the exponent, and set out how to test whether the resulting framework also applies to AI. The runs recorded here test none of its laws (Section 3). The mathematics is old. The framework’s reading of it and its extension to AI are new, and both are hypotheses under test.

1.8 Why this matters: for everyone

If you use AI at all, how AI is evaluated affects you. Much published evaluation of AI systems relies on model judges, and in this record a direction such judges reported did not hold from one protocol to the next, in runs that also differed in other ways (Eastwood 2026a).

If you care about the future, AI may become the most powerful technology humanity has created. Whether it helps or harms us depends on whether we can make it ethical. This notebook records one attempt to measure whether longer reasoning makes it so, with its defects stated.

If you are a scientist: any evaluation in which a model judge can see or infer whose output it is scoring is exposed to this kind of bias. Earlier studies documented related biases (Zheng et al. 2023; Panickssery et al. 2024; Dubois et al. 2024; Saraf et al. 2025). If Paper XII’s test, once registered and run, finds blinding reordering models on a public benchmark, comparisons that rest on unblinded model judges would need re-checking. If blinding moves scores but not rankings, which is that paper’s own forecast, it matters for measurement precision rather than for leaderboard order (Eastwood 2026h).

If you are a policymaker, regulations built on the assumption that “more capable AI is more aligned AI” would, if these data were replicated, need re-examining at least for reasoning depth. In this run, longer reasoning did not raise every model’s judged scores.

1.9 Historical comparisons

To help non-specialist readers understand the type of contribution each discovery represents, the following table offers loose analogies, imperfect but illustrative. These comparisons describe the category of finding, not its confirmed significance. Whether they prove apt depends on independent replication.

Table 3. Loose analogies for the kinds of finding recorded here; each row is corrected, and Appendix E.3 records each correction.
This finding Is comparable to Why
Unblinded rises that did not hold under a changed protocol Introduction of double-blind trials in medicine (1940s to 1960s) Before blinding, doctors “knew” which treatments worked based on uncontrolled observations. Blinding revealed that many “proven” treatments were useless or harmful. If a controlled test showed blinding to be the cause, this would mean that AI safety evaluation has a similar methodological gap: results that appear valid but do not hold under proper controls.
Capability and judged alignment moved differently Separation of IQ and emotional intelligence (1990s) If replicated across models and runs, it would show that mathematical accuracy and judged ethical reasoning can move in opposite directions within one model as reasoning depth grows. One run does not show that they are separate dimensions (Eastwood 2026d).
The Cauchy unification of d/(d+1)d/(d+1) Showing that results derived separately share a common root Earlier work derived an exponent of this form, each in its own domain and terms (Section 2). The framework’s reading relates these results to Cauchy’s functional equation and extends it to AI scaling. Cauchy’s equations restrict a functional family, not the exponent, so the shared root is a hypothesis under test, not a demonstration, and a unification, not an original discovery of the formula.
Sequential >> parallel (thinking deeply beats thinking widely) Careful step-by-step reasoning against a crowd’s guesses Asking 100 people to guess an answer (parallel) is less effective than one person thinking carefully through each step (sequential). In Paper II’s tier-2 arm, sequential exceeded parallel wherever both exponents could be estimated, and the two arms were not matched for compute (Eastwood 2026c). If replicated with the two arms matched for compute, it would support the framework’s sequential-over-parallel prediction; a derivable exponent needs the premises Section 2 states.
The Eden Protocol’s stakeholder-care result A simple procedural change whose effect looks obvious only in retrospect A simple intervention, asking “who does this affect?” before answering, raised scored stakeholder care in all five analysable runs of a partially blind pilot (Eastwood 2026n). If replicated blind, this would mean a low-cost technique exists for improving one judged dimension of AI alignment.
