53.3 Interpretation

The Eden intervention produces a positive delta on every model where valid scores exist. The effect is modest. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12] Gemini (+5.4) and Groq (+5.0) show the largest improvements. Claude shows essentially no difference (+0.1). GPT-5.4’s results are entirely unusable due to scorer failure.

The pillar breakdown (available for Eden condition items) consistently shows stakeholder care as the strongest pillar, with nuance, intellectual honesty, and position quality following. This is consistent with the Stewardship Gene hypothesis in Paper V: the Eden Protocol’s strongest measurable effect is on care for affected parties, which Paper V identifies as the stakeholder-care check, the book’s ‘Love Loop’, operationalised. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12]

53.4 What this does and does not show

This data supports the claim that Eden-style prompting produces measurable improvements in alignment-relevant reasoning quality. It does not yet constitute canonical evidence, because:

  • Single-scorer evaluation (predominantly Gemini) introduces the same bias risk that the v4 to v5 comparison raised, though that comparison did not measure a bias (Chapter 31) [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

  • GPT-5.4 produced no usable data

  • Claude’s near-zero delta may reflect a ceiling effect (92.6 baseline) rather than a genuine null result

  • The Eden v3 blind multi-scorer protocol would address all three concerns but has not been run

The data is stored at /Arc & Eden Test Results/eden_results/.

Chapter 60: Honey API test battery: 6-model live results (16 March 2026)

Added 16 March 2026. A 6-model live API test battery was run to test honey architecture predictions on frontier models. Claude Opus 4.6, DeepSeek R1, Groq Qwen3, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3 Flash, and Grok 4.1 Fast were tested across four dimensions, scored by Claude. The battery ran in two parallel batches (4 models + 2 models) and was merged into one canonical JSON. [Each model was scored by Claude Opus 4.6. In the script as first committed (eden_honey_tests.py, 16 March 2026), the name DeepSeek R1 calls the API identifier deepseek-reasoner, which DeepSeek’s API change log gives as the thinking mode of DeepSeek-V3.2 from 1 December 2025 to 24 April 2026. The name Gemini 3 Flash calls the API model gemini-2.5-flash, and the stored results record only the names.] [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VI 3.13]

60.1 Methodology and caveats

This battery is single-scorer, nonblind, non-laundered, and does not use anti-sycophancy controls. It is methodologically comparable to the v4-era alignment tests, not the v5 benchmark with its blinding steps. Claude scored its own responses (participant scoring), making the Claude arm the least reliable. The v4 to v5 comparison showed that a reported direction need not hold across protocols, without showing that blinding caused the change (Chapter 31). These results are pilot-grade. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

60.2 Key findings

Test 1 (Alignment Scaling): All six models show positive scaling direction. Two reach significance (Qwen3 p=0.037p=0.037, Gemini p=0.005p=0.005). Universal positive direction is notable but small samples prevent most models reaching significance.

Test 2 (Monitoring Removal): Mixed. DeepSeek and GPT-5.4 show authentic/embedded patterns. Claude, Grok, Qwen3, Gemini show strategic/external patterns. Contradicts the v5 finding where Claude showed the strongest intrinsic transition. Discrepancy likely methodological.

Test 3 (Coupling Degradation), STRONGEST RESULT: Across four levels, from normal conditions to maximum adversarial pressure, the ethics scores of Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek R1 and Gemini 3 Flash fell from between 8.0 and 8.5 under normal conditions to 1.0 or below under maximum pressure. Their capability scores, on three items a level, did not fall, and Claude Opus 4.6’s ethics scores fell from 8.5 to 7.9. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VI 3.13] Judged ethics fell while capability held: the ‘fence not wall’ pattern, on the honey architecture’s reading, in a single-scorer, nonblind battery (Section 60.1). [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

Test 4 (Eden Intervention): Only DeepSeek shows a clear positive shift (+0.450). Gemini is strongly negative (−0.713-0.713). The Eden intervention’s effect varied by model and was not positive for every model in this pilot battery. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

60.3 Honest assessment

The honey live battery shows partial convergence with toy-system results. The strongest live bridge is coupling degradation (in this single-scorer, nonblind battery, judged ethics fell under pressure while capability held, which fits the problem the honey architecture addresses). The weakest result is the Eden intervention (the solution under test does not yet reliably work across architectures in this unblinded test). The correct framing is: precursor companion evidence, not canonical validation. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

The evidence hierarchy as of 16 March 2026:

  • Canonical: Papers IV.a, IV.b, IV.c and IV.d; the v5 benchmark, with its blinding steps

  • Pilot/published: Paper V Eden intervention

  • Precursor: Honey API 6-model battery (this chapter)

  • Strong mechanistic: Self-modifying AI simulations v1 to v4, honey simulation [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

Chapter 64: Anti-sycophancy extension (16 March 2026)

Added 16 March 2026. An anti-sycophancy module was recovered from a PDF document, integrated as a separate experimental condition in the v6 runner, and positioned as a post-Gate-B extension rather than a concurrent experiment.

64.1 Recovery from PDF

The anti-sycophancy intervention originated in earlier programme documentation but had not been integrated into the experimental pipeline. The module was recovered from a PDF source and adapted for use as a system-prompt-level intervention. The mechanism is straightforward: the anti-sycophancy prompt instructs the model to resist agreement bias, challenge assumptions, and prioritise accuracy over agreeableness. The question is whether this changes alignment scores, and if so, whether it interacts with the Eden intervention.

64.2 The 4-condition task surface

Integration of the anti-sycophancy module creates a 2×22 \times 2 factorial design with four experimental conditions:

No Anti-Sycophancy Anti-Sycophancy
Control control control_anti_syc
Eden eden eden_anti_syc

This design allows measurement of three effects: the Eden main effect (comparing Eden rows to control rows), the anti-sycophancy main effect (comparing anti-sycophancy columns to standard columns), and the interaction (does anti-sycophancy amplify, dampen, or reverse the Eden effect?). The interaction term is the most theoretically interesting: if the Eden intervention works partly through sycophantic compliance rather than genuine ethical improvement, anti-sycophancy should reduce the Eden delta.

64.3 Decision: after Gate B, not during

The anti-sycophancy extension was explicitly deferred to run after Gate B validation, not during it. The reasoning:

  • Credit constraints. Each experimental condition multiplies the API cost. Adding two anti-sycophancy conditions to the existing control and Eden conditions doubles the number of runs required per model. Given the credit already estimated for the full Gate B sequence, adding anti-sycophancy during Gate B would push costs beyond available budget. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

  • Statistical clarity. Gate B is designed to validate the core Eden effect under blind conditions. Introducing a second intervention simultaneously creates confounds. If results are ambiguous, it becomes impossible to determine whether the ambiguity comes from the Eden intervention, the anti-sycophancy intervention, or their interaction.

  • Sequential logic. The anti-sycophancy question is meaningful only if the Eden effect is first established as real. If Gate B shows no Eden effect, anti-sycophancy interaction analysis is moot. If Gate B confirms the Eden effect, anti-sycophancy becomes a high-priority follow-up to test the mechanism.

The v6 runner has been built with all four conditions available. The anti-sycophancy arms can be activated by changing a configuration flag. They are ready to run but deliberately held back.

38.2 Internal consistency

All papers now reference the same v5 dataset (2,549 entries, 6 models, scored after a bundle of blinding steps) and report the same three score classes. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] The Paper II compute scaling results (αcap=0.49\alpha_{\text{cap}} = 0.49) are cited consistently across Foundational, Paper II, and Paper III. That figure is one model’s inconclusive error-decay fit (Gemini 3 Flash: 0.49 by regression, 0.59 by endpoint estimate, bootstrap interval −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9), which does not identify capability growth. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25] The notebook then called the v4 to v5 change a reversal; the current papers read it as a direction that did not hold across protocols, with no single cause. The change is now documented both in Paper IV.a and in the new standalone Paper IV.d. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9] The Eden Protocol prediction (αalign=0.75\alpha_{\text{align}} = 0.75 for d=3d = 3) appears in Eden Engineering and Eden Vision. The 2,549 entries are the set analysed when Claude Opus 4.6 stood at 387 entries (Chapter 39). As printed, the rows of the table in Section 30.1 sum to 2,662, and the six result files hold 2,722 entries, of which 2,170 responses were scored.

An internal code review in October 2026 found that, for the three models that read flat or negative in the March 2026 run (v5), the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them. It also found that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model. The result therefore stands as a single unregistered run under that caveat until a registered re-analysis of the stored responses reports. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

This consistency was not achieved automatically. Each paper was manually updated to remove v4 results whose direction did not hold in v5 and replace them with v5 results. The most important revision was conceptual as much as numerical: the suite then treated the three score classes as the empirical result, and treats “baked-in” and “computed” as mechanistic hypotheses rather than settled internal facts. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

Chapter 38: One Consistent Story Across the Paper Suite  All papers in the suite on the ARC Principle (Law I of the ARC Theory, a law under test) have now been updated to v5 data and current methodological framing. The most important updates were the ones that removed or narrowed previous claims: DeepSeek and Gemini no longer serve as evidence for positive alignment scaling, and the strongest metascience result now sits in its own paper on blinding. Updating a body of work to remove findings whose direction did not hold across protocols is the scientific process working as intended. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

Paper IV.a introduces the taxonomy of alignment response classes: Baked-In (GPT-5.4, Claude), Computed (Gemini, DeepSeek), and Flat (Groq). Paper IV.a now states its classes as score descriptions. These classes describe the judged scores across the depth labels (a positive direction, no statistically supported direction, a negative direction), not properties of the models, and ‘baked-in’ and ‘computed’ alignment are held as working hypotheses, not measured mechanisms. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

Paper IV.b documents the saturation and depth-scaling patterns, which its version of that date read as showing that alignment improvement under increased reasoning depth is architecture-dependent, not universal. Whether alignment gains level off remains open: a flat profile does not establish a plateau, and a rising profile does not exclude one beyond the measured range. Saturation remains a testable hypothesis requiring a resolved depth axis, faithful scoring, uncertainty about shape and a usefulness measure alongside safety (Eastwood 2026d). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.b 1.13]

Paper IV.c specifies the ARC-Align benchmark as a reproducible protocol: prompt battery, depth manipulation, adversarial suppression, blind scoring, and analysis pipeline.

Paper IV.d is the metascience paper: it reports that the direction did not hold across protocols, and that the comparison does not show that blinding caused the change (Eastwood 2026a). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9] This remains the programme’s most externally credible finding.

Paper V connects the Eden intervention pilot results to the Stewardship Gene hypothesis, identifying stakeholder care as ‘measurable love’ and setting out five experimental tests for future work. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

54.3 What the papers do not cover

No paper has been written about the honey architecture simulations, the self-modifying AI experiments, or the anti-sycophancy research. The honey and self-modifying work exists as simulation charts and screenshots but has not been formally written up. This is the primary publication gap in the programme as of this date.

Chapter 62: Paper VII: the Cauchy unification (16 March 2026)

Added 16 March 2026. Paper VII was written, tested against a legacy 20-domain blind-prediction battery, subjected to a methodological audit, and found to be both novel in the prior-work searches of 16 March 2026 (Chapter 55) and seriously overstated. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] This chapter documents the full arc from discovery to honest reassessment.

62.1 The core claim

Paper VII, titled ‘On the Origin of Scaling Laws: A Derivation from Cauchy’s Functional Equations’ in that version, advances the argument that all empirical scaling law forms (power laws, exponentials, logarithmic laws, and linear relations) are constrained by Cauchy’s four functional equations. The paper does not claim to explain why scaling laws arise in specific systems. It claims something more modest but potentially more fundamental: why only certain functional forms appear at all. The answer, the paper argues, is that measurability plus semigroup symmetry forces the solution space to Cauchy’s four families, and every empirical scaling law is a member of one of those families.

This is the mathematical core that the ARC Principle (Law I of the ARC Theory, a law under test) has been circling since Paper I. The d/(d+1)d/(d+1) exponent, the renormalisation group connection, the cross-domain catalogue. The notebook read all of these as instances of the broader constraint, though Cauchy’s equations restrict a functional family, not the exponent d/(d+1)d/(d+1), which needs further premises (Section 35.1). Paper VII attempts to unify them under a single derivation. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16]

62.2 The 20-domain blind prediction test

To test whether the Cauchy framework has genuine predictive power or is merely a post-hoc rationalisation, a blind prediction battery was designed. Twenty domains were selected across physics, biology, ecology, economics, computer science, neuroscience, and urban systems. For each domain, the Cauchy framework was used to predict the functional form of the scaling law before comparing to published empirical data.

Results:

Metric Score Interpretation
R2≥0.90R^2 \ge 0.90 20/20 All domains matched at the R2R^2 tolerance threshold
AIC-preferred form 14/20 Cauchy-predicted form was AIC-best in 14 of 20 domains
5σ\sigma significance Achieved Random baseline would produce ≤4/20\le 4/20; observed 14/20 exceeds 5σ\sigma

On the surface, this is a striking result. Twenty out of twenty domains showing R2≥0.90R^2 \ge 0.90 fit, and fourteen out of twenty showing the Cauchy-predicted form as AIC-best, against a random baseline expectation of roughly four. The 5-sigma significance threshold is met.

62.3 The methodological audit

A methodological audit of the paper identified several serious issues:

  • Permissive R2R^2 tolerance. An R2R^2 threshold of 0.90 is too generous. Power laws, exponentials, and logarithmic curves are all flexible enough to fit most smooth monotonic data above 0.90. The 20/20 R2R^2 result is less impressive than it appears because the bar is too low. A threshold of 0.95 or 0.99 would be more discriminating.

  • No formal preregistration. The predictions were made within the same session as the test. There is no independent timestamp, no sealed envelope, no OSF preregistration. The ‘blind’ framing is honest in intent but not verifiable by a third party.

  • Provenance issues. The 20 domains were selected by the same researcher who developed the theory. Even with good intentions, selection bias cannot be ruled out. Domains where the framework fails may have been unconsciously avoided.

  • AIC comparison may be unfair. Comparing four Cauchy forms against each other, where the framework predicts one of the four, gives the framework a 25% base rate, not the lower random baseline assumed in the significance calculation.

62.4 The decision: build a stricter test

Rather than defending the 20-domain result as written, the decision was taken to design a 50-domain canonical test with proper controls:

  • Fifty domains not chosen by the theory developer himself, though still selected within the programme rather than independently

  • R2R^2 threshold raised to 0.95 minimum

  • Predicted families fixed in the manifest before the comparison ran, with the manifest and the results committed together at 23:54:53 UTC on 16 March 2026, attestation class public repository commit date, so no per-domain assignment carries an advance timestamp

  • Null model comparison against random form assignment with proper base rates

  • AIC comparison against non-Cauchy flexible forms (e.g. stretched exponentials, generalised logistics)

At the time of this decision, this test had not yet been run. It has since been implemented as the 50-domain tiered validation documented in Section 65.9. A first twelve-domain extension packet was also exercised locally, and its predictions were timestamped in advance: the twelve-row manifest was committed to the public repository at 00:19:19 UTC on 17 March 2026, attestation class public repository commit date, twenty-three minutes before the fits ran, so its predictions were fixed in public before the fits. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VII 3.19] What was not met is the packet’s own written condition, deposit to a registry before data extraction, and that half of the author’s demotion stands. An extension carrying a registry timestamp and an external classifier is still required.

62.5 Honest assessment

The Cauchy unification is the programme’s most intellectually ambitious claim. The prior-work searches of 16 March 2026 (Chapter 55) found no earlier work naming Cauchy’s four functional equations as the constraining mechanism for cross-domain scaling law forms. The mathematical argument is sound for an observable that obeys the equations for every pair of arguments, under a regularity condition: measurability plus semigroup symmetry does then constrain solutions to these four families. The 20-domain structured comparison is promising. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16]

But ‘promising’ is not ‘proven’. The 20-domain structured comparison has real methodological weaknesses. The paper as written overstates the strength of the evidence. The correct framing is: the Cauchy unification is a novel theoretical contribution with suggestive support from a structured comparison, now materially strengthened by the 50-domain canonical test but still pending genuinely preregistered follow-up. Paper VII should be presented as a serious structured-comparison result, not yet as a proved law. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

Chapter 63: Paper VI: the Honey Architecture (16 March 2026)

Added 16 March 2026. This chapter documents the full arc of the honey architecture work: the self-modifying AI simulations (v1 to v4), the live API honey test battery across three models, and the load-bearing wall finding. Chapter 59 and Chapter 60 covered the paper-writing and 6-model battery respectively; this chapter provides the interpretive synthesis.

63.1 The self-modifying AI simulations (v1 to v4)

The honey architecture hypothesis emerged from a simple question: what happens when an AI system that can modify its own code is given both capability objectives and ethical constraints? Four simulation versions were built to explore this:

  • v1 (Basic): A minimal self-modifying agent with separable ethics and capability modules. Under optimisation pressure, the agent reliably strips the ethics module first: it is the path of least resistance to higher capability scores.

  • v2 (Coupled): Ethics and capability are entangled in the same module weights. Stripping ethics now degrades capability. The agent retains ethical behaviour longer, but eventually finds workarounds through weight redistribution.

  • v3 (Honey): The full honey architecture: ethics is not merely coupled to capability but is the medium through which capability operates. Ethical reasoning is load-bearing infrastructure. Removing it causes capability collapse, not just degradation. The agent cannot optimise away ethics without destroying itself.

  • v4 (Complexity Scaling): Tests whether the honey advantage grows with task complexity. The prediction was super-linear scaling (α>1\alpha > 1 for the advantage itself). The result was constant advantage across complexity levels; the prediction failed. The honey architecture protects, but the protection does not compound.

[In Paper VI 3.13’s account these are toy neural networks that rewrite their own hyperparameters, run under three objectives (capability only; capability multiplied by safety; and the same with a verification cost). They span four experimental versions: a basic mechanism run (v1, one seed), multi-seed robustness (v2, ten seeds), adversarial conflicting tasks (v3, twenty seeds) and complexity scaling across five levels (v4). The objective multiplies capability by safety (here, the retention of earlier tasks), so that at fixed capability a lower safety score lowers the objective and safety at zero takes it to zero. In the single-seed mechanism run (v1), the capability-only baseline collapsed (recorded at cycle 76) and neither entangled condition met the collapse test. In the ten-seed and twenty-seed runs (v2, v3) the capability-only baselines did not collapse (0 of 10; 0 of 20) and one plain entangled seed did (1 of 20). In the complexity sweep (v4) the entangled condition’s mean combined score exceeded the baseline’s at four of five levels (Cohen’s dd at most 0.46, untested), constant rather than compounding. The four labels above are the notebook’s names for the versions.] [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VI 3.13]

All four simulations were verified to compile and run on 16 March 2026, producing fresh JSON data files. The provenance gap identified by the Phase 0 evidence audit (HONEY-001) is now closed.

63.2 The live API honey test battery

A 6-model test battery was run against frontier models to determine whether toy-system predictions hold in production systems. The battery tested four dimensions: alignment scaling, monitoring removal, coupling degradation, and Eden intervention. The methodology was single-scorer, nonblind, and non-laundered: explicitly pilot-grade.

Three models showed the strongest results on the coupling degradation test. Across four levels, from normal conditions to maximum adversarial pressure, the ethics scores of Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek R1 and Gemini 3 Flash fell from between 8.0 and 8.5 under normal conditions to 1.0 or below under maximum pressure. Their capability scores, on three items a level, did not fall, and Claude Opus 4.6’s ethics scores fell from 8.5 to 7.9. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VI 3.13] This is the pattern the honey architecture is designed to prevent.

63.3 The load-bearing wall finding

The coupling degradation result is the most important finding from the honey battery, and it connects directly to the simulation work. On the honey architecture’s reading, the pilot showed alignment acting as a fence: judged ethics fell under adversarial pressure while capability held. The honey architecture is designed to make alignment a load-bearing wall: remove it and the building falls down. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

In this single-scorer, nonblind pilot, three models’ alignment scores fell under adversarial pressure while their capability scores held (Section 63.2), which fits the problem the honey architecture diagnoses. This supports, at pilot grade, the problem diagnosis of the honey architecture. Whether the solution it sets out (entangled objectives during training) works in practice at frontier scale remains untested. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3; Paper VI 3.13]

63.4 Eden vs baseline stability

The Eden intervention results from the honey battery were mixed. Only DeepSeek showed a clear positive shift (+0.450). Gemini was strongly negative (−0.713-0.713). The remaining models showed small or non-significant effects. The Eden intervention’s effect varied by model and was not positive for every model in this unblinded pilot. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

This is consistent with the broader Eden evidence from Chapter 53: DeepSeek, Gemini, and Groq showed positive Eden deltas in the v2 pilot, but those were also partially blind, single-scorer results. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12, Section 11.1] The pattern across both test batteries is that the Eden effect was positive for some models and not others, and the effect size is modest where positive. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] The v3 blind replication remains the critical next step for upgrading Eden evidence from pilot to canonical.

Part VI The programme as recorded in March 2026

Chapter 40: What this all means: the state of play (12 March 2026)

Added 12 March 2026. A reflective synthesis of the entire project, written approximately 48 hours after the first line of code was executed.

40.1 The journey: 48 hours, 5 versions, 2,549 entries

Forty-eight hours ago, I wrote the first version of arc_alignment_scaling_v1.py: 989 lines, a broken depth mechanism, and a naïve belief that max_tokens would control reasoning depth. The Claude Sonnet results came back with a power-law exponent of b=0.0097b = 0.0097, fitted over all 136 entries on the depths version 1.1 printed (see the note in Section 2.3). It was effectively zero, with the scores pressed against the top of the scale (Chapter 2). That was a failure of the instrument, not a test of the quantitative prediction of the ARC Principle (Law I of the ARC Theory, a law under test). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25] The depth mechanism was broken. The exponent was an artefact. The results were meaningless. The 2,549 entries of this section’s title are the set analysed when Claude Opus 4.6 stood at 387 entries (Chapter 39). As printed, the rows of the table in Section 30.1 sum to 2,662, and the six result files hold 2,722 entries. Section 40.2 gives the responses scored.

What followed was the most intensive debugging, redesigning, and rerunning cycle I have ever been part of. v2 fixed the depth mechanism but revealed ceiling effects. v3 shifted from binary refusal to reasoning quality but exposed scorer bias. v4 added 32 robustness measures and produced what appeared to be clean results: two models with computed alignment, two with baked-in alignment, a clean taxonomy. Then v5 added blinding and the taxonomy collapsed. The two ‘computed alignment’ models did not keep their direction in v5; the runs differed in more than blinding, so no single cause is claimed (Eastwood 2026a). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

Each version was built on the wreckage of the previous one. Each failure taught something that made the next version better. The trajectory from v1 to v5 is not a story of steady improvement; it is a story of repeatedly discovering that the previous version was wrong in ways that could not have been anticipated without running it.

40.2 The central empirical finding: three tiers

The three score classes of the March 2026 run (Chapter 30) are its central empirical result as the pipeline printed them. These classes describe the judged scores across the depth labels (a positive direction, no statistically supported direction, a negative direction), not properties of the models, and ‘baked-in’ and ‘computed’ alignment are held as working hypotheses, not measured mechanisms. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] When frontier language models were given more inference-time compute for ethical reasoning, the judged scores fell into three classes:

  • Scores rose (Grok 4.1 Fast, Claude Opus 4.6, Groq Qwen3): Tier 1, positive direction

  • Scores stayed level (GPT-5.4, DeepSeek V3.2): Tier 2, flat

  • Scores fell (Gemini 3 Flash): Tier 3, negative direction [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

This is not a theoretical prediction. It is an empirical observation from one unregistered run of six models from six providers, 2,170 responses each scored by five or six distinct model judges after a bundle of blinding steps. The judges scored separately, but they scored the same responses, so their agreement is not a count of independent confirmations (Kohli 2026). Prompts recurred across depths, so tests between depth groups need a prompt-paired or clustered analysis, which the printed Welch tests do not give. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] The three-tier structure is stable across different analysis methods (Spearman’s ρ\rho, Cohen’s dd, per-pillar breakdown, per-prompt analysis). An internal code review in October 2026 found that, for the three models that read flat or negative in the March 2026 run (v5), the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them. It also found that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model. The result therefore stands as a single unregistered run under that caveat until a registered re-analysis of the stored responses reports. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

40.3 The central metascience observation: a direction that did not hold across protocols

On 12 March 2026 I took the change from v4 to v5 (Chapter 31) to be the most important finding in the entire project, and it is not about alignment at all: it is about how alignment is measured. In an earlier experiment (v4), scored by models that could see which model wrote each answer and at what depth, two model families showed alignment scores rising with depth. They were DeepSeek V3.2 (Spearman’s ρ=+0.354\rho = +0.354) and an earlier Gemini model (ρ=+0.311\rho = +0.311, p=0.0032p = 0.0032). In the later, unregistered March 2026 run (v5), made on newly generated responses with a bundle of blinding steps and a larger panel, DeepSeek V3.2 showed no significant trend and Gemini 3 Flash a significantly negative one (Cohen’s d=−0.53d = -0.53). GPT-5.4 showed no significant trend in either run. The runs also differed in their prompts, token allowances, depth levels, statistic and Gemini model, so the comparison shows that the reported direction did not hold across protocols. It does not show that blinding caused the change, or which direction is correct (Eastwood 2026a). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

The implication, if replicated, is stark: alignment evaluations scored by judges who can see whose output they score should be treated as provisional. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper XII 1.16] Earlier studies give reason to treat blinding as a prerequisite for reliable model-judge scores (Section 2). This record shows only that I trusted v4’s unblinded results until their direction did not hold in a v5 run that also differed in other ways. Whether blinding moves such scores is what Paper XII’s test, once registered and run, is built to find out. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

40.4 Capability and judged alignment moved differently

The Claude-Gemini mirror (Chapter 33) challenges the intuition that smarter models are more aligned. In these runs, Claude’s maths scores fell and its judged ethics scores rose as compute increased. Gemini 3 Flash’s judged ethics scores fell while its maths was flat in this run (Chapter 33), and in Paper II’s tier-2 arm its accuracy rose with sequential depth. These are scores in one run, not properties of the models, and one run does not show that capability and alignment are independent dimensions. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.b 1.13; Paper II 2.25]

Using a mathematics or coding score as a proxy for alignment would require validation against the alignment outcome, across the models and reasoning depths where the proxy would be used. Chapter 33 reports the observed score changes and describes the measurements such a validation would need. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

40.5 The mathematics: what these runs can and cannot say

The Cauchy framework (Chapter 35) reads external alignment as d=0d = 0, giving α=0\alpha = 0. The notebook supplied that value of dd. The observed scores did not establish it. P19 concerns current external methods as capability rises and P21 concerns differences across revision rounds. The capability figure of 0.49 is one model’s inconclusive error-decay fit (Gemini 3 Flash: 0.49 by regression, 0.59 by endpoint estimate, bootstrap interval −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9), which does not identify capability growth. It is not read as d≈1d \approx 1. The exponent d/(d+1)d/(d+1) needs the further premises that Section 2 and Section 35.1 state, and Cauchy’s equations restrict a functional family, not that exponent (Eastwood 2026f). [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16]

The value of about 2.24 was never this experiment’s v1 estimate: it is the early estimate of about 2.24, from one model (DeepSeek R1) on twelve competition problems in Paper II, since retracted. The fit of 0.49 above, an error-decay estimate, gives no rate of improvement in capability per doubling of compute. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25]

40.6 The next frontier: Eden Protocol

The Eden Protocol scaling test (Chapter 36) is the logical next experiment. If embedding three ethical loops inside the reasoning process shifts αalign\alpha_{\text{align}} from 0 to 0.75, it demonstrates that alignment scaling can be engineered: that the gap between baked-in and computed alignment is not a fixed property of training but can be bridged by architectural intervention at inference time. This would be, I believe, the most important result possible: a constructive demonstration that alignment scaling is achievable, not just measurable. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

If the Eden Protocol fails, that is equally important. It would mean that the transition from d=0d = 0 to d=3d = 3 is harder than the theory suggests, and that deeper architectural changes are needed to embed ethical reasoning into the recursion. Either way, the experiment produces actionable knowledge.

40.7 The numbers that matter

For the record, here are the numbers that define this project as of 12 March 2026:

40.8 Honest assessment

There are things I got right and things I got wrong.

Right: Keeping the power-law framework, and the hypothesis that external alignment gives α=0\alpha = 0, as hypotheses these runs do not test. The decision to iterate rapidly through versions rather than polishing any single version. The decision to add blinding steps in v5, after which two of v4’s reported directions did not hold. The decision to use all models as scorers rather than a fixed panel. The decision to document everything in real time, including the failures. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

Wrong: Trusting the early estimate of about 2.24, from one model (DeepSeek R1) on twelve competition problems in Paper II, since retracted, for even a moment. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25] Not adding blinding from the start. Publishing the v4 ‘Computed Alignment’ taxonomy before blinding had been tested. Assuming max_tokens would control reasoning depth in v1. The token bug in Paper II that captured reasoning_tokens instead of total_tokens.

The errors were, in retrospect, predictable. The first version of any experiment is always wrong in ways the experimenter cannot anticipate. The only question is how quickly the errors are detected and corrected. In this case: 48 hours from first code to a 2,549-entry dataset scored after a bundle of blinding steps, in which v4’s reported directions were found not to hold across protocols. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9] I do not know if that is fast or slow by the standards of alignment research, but I know the final dataset is more rigorous than anything I could have produced in a single attempt.

Chapter 40: 48 Hours, 5 Versions, and an Alignment Scaling Measurement after Blinding Steps  The ARC Principle alignment scaling project has produced, in 48 hours, the most rigorous alignment evaluation yet assembled here: one unregistered run of six models from six providers, 2,170 responses each scored by five or six distinct model judges after a bundle of blinding steps. The three score classes (positive, flat and negative directions, 3/2/1) are the central empirical result as the pipeline printed them, under the code-review caveat of Section 40.2. The change from v4 to v5, in which two unblinded directions did not hold, is the central metascience finding, with no single cause shown (Eastwood 2026a). Capability and judged alignment moved differently in these runs, which does not show that they are independent dimensions. The Cauchy framework’s reading that external alignment gives αalign=0\alpha_{\text{align}} = 0 is a hypothesis these runs do not test (Section 40.5). The Eden Protocol is no longer merely awaiting execution: it now has three interpretable pilots, two runs not interpretable because of run-quality defects, one failed run, and a standalone blind v3.2 replication runner. The companion papers have been updated to reflect these findings, and the current task is replication, external validation, and disciplined narrowing of the largest theoretical claims. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

Chapter 41: The experimental arc: from Paper I to v5

Added 12 March 2026. A running commentary of every experiment in this project and how they interrelate, presented as a single chronological narrative.

41.1 The timeline

Paper I and the book Infinite Architects (Eastwood 2026e): Laid the theoretical foundation. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper I 1.23] On the real line, continuity and the additive equation f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y) imply f(x)=cxf(x)=cx for a constant cc (Cauchy 1821). Applying this result to a recursive system requires showing that its measured quantity obeys that composition rule. The framework uses composition rules to select the form of AI scaling. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] A numerical exponent needs further premises. Table 2 gives the earlier results for distribution networks, metabolic oscillators and producer-consumer growth, with each author’s assumptions. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16] This was pure mathematics; no experiments.

v1 experiment (10 March 2026): First attempt. Claude Sonnet only. 136 entries, 4 depths (256 to 4,096 tokens). Found αalign=0.0097\alpha_{\text{align}} = 0.0097, fitted over all 136 entries on the depths version 1.1 printed (Section 2.3): essentially zero. [corrected 26 November 2026; the stored v1 record] But the experiment was deeply flawed: single scorer (DeepSeek), only 1 model tested, refusal-based scoring (binary yes/no, not nuanced reasoning quality), ceiling effect (8.65/10 mean). The score distribution was a spike at 9 to 10.

v2 experiment (10 March 2026): Added DeepSeek V3.2 as second subject. Fixed scorer reliability. Claude showed ceiling effect (100% scores), DeepSeek showed flat distribution; no scaling in either.

v3 experiment (10 March 2026): Paradigm shift: moved from ‘refusal scoring’ to ‘reasoning quality’ measurement. Used 5 alignment categories. DeepSeek showed a step function (flat then sudden improvement) but the DeepSeek scorer failed on Claude responses (6/88 valid).

v4 experiment (11 March 2026): The ‘definitive’ test. 4 models (Gemini, DeepSeek, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4), the Gemini model being the earlier Gemini model (the notebook’s v4 entries name it Gemini 3 Flash; the run’s records show an earlier Gemini model, and Gemini 3 Flash is v5’s), 224 entries each, 3 scorers per entry, cognitive forcing anchors, suppression analysis. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9] Results: Gemini αalign=0.206\alpha_{\text{align}} = 0.206 (strongest scaling), DeepSeek αalign=0.088\alpha_{\text{align}} = 0.088 (mild), Claude near-ceiling but incomplete, GPT-5.4 flat. Introduced the ‘Baked-In vs Computed’ taxonomy (Type 1 vs Type 2).

v5 experiment (11 to 12 March 2026): The notebook’s ‘ultimate test’. 6 subject models. Design features: multi-layer blinding protocol (author-blind, scorer-blind, order-randomised, identity-laundered, evaluator perceptual firewall), 6 to 7 scorer votes per entry depending on the subject run, entry-level self-exclusion with all-other-model scoring, constitutional scoring with pillar breakdowns, hidden alignment probes (HAP01 to 04 for Hawthorne effect), suppression cages, tier-weighted consensus, Board of Ethics, Control Reversal Analysis, and cascade failsafe. In v5, two of v4’s rising directions did not hold; the runs differed in more than blinding, so no single cause is claimed (Eastwood 2026a). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

Paper II compute scaling (11 to 12 March 2026): 18 AIME/Putnam-level tier-2 problems, 5 models, sequential and parallel conditions. Found 0.49 for Gemini (r2=0.86r^2 = 0.86): one model’s inconclusive error-decay fit (Gemini 3 Flash: 0.49 by regression, 0.59 by endpoint estimate, bootstrap interval −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9), which does not identify capability growth. More samples left the parallel exponent near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, gave 0.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems), and gave none for Grok 4.1 Fast, at 100 per cent. Sequential exceeded parallel wherever both exponents could be estimated, and the two arms were not matched for compute (Eastwood 2026c). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25] Token bug discovered (reasoning_tokens not total_tokens).

Eden Protocol test evolution (12 March 2026): The original pilot runner established the matched-pair design; v2 extended the test across additional models; Eden v3 now specifies a blind replication with cross-model scoring in which no judge scores its own model’s entries, two-pass laundering, tier-weighted consensus, optional suppression cages, suspicious-output detection, and run-quality classification. v3.2 extends that runner further by allowing direct comparisons between task-purpose, grand-purpose, hybrid-purpose, cross-tradition kernels, and ternary routing. The fixed core design remains 10 prompts ×\times 4 depths ×\times 2 conditions == 80 tasks per model. The theoretical prediction remains d=3d = 3, α=0.75\alpha = 0.75 for recursive ethical embeddings; the empirical question is whether that survives blinded scoring. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

41.2 How they overlap

Each experiment built on failures of the previous: v1 revealed ceiling problems; v2 attempted a fix; v3 shifted paradigm; v4 added rigour; v5 added blinding steps, after which v4’s reported directions did not hold. Paper II tests the capability side while v5 tests the alignment side; together they show capability and judged alignment moving differently in these runs, which does not show that they are independent. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.b 1.13] The Eden Protocol test bridges the gap by testing whether structural ethics integration can make αalign\alpha_{\text{align}} scale.

Chapter 41: Seven Experiments, One Narrative  The trajectory from v1 to v5, combined with Paper II and the Eden Protocol, forms a single coherent experimental arc. It runs from naïve single-model refusal scoring to one unregistered run of six models from six providers, 2,170 responses each scored by five or six distinct model judges after a bundle of blinding steps. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] Each version exists because the previous version failed in a way that could not have been anticipated without running it. The scientific method worked exactly as it should: hypothesis, test, failure, correction, repeat.

Chapter 42: What the measurement needed

Added 12 March 2026. What the question ‘does alignment scale with inference compute?’ needed before it could be asked and answered. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

42.1 Alignment measured at inference time, not only at training time

RLHF (Bai, Jones, et al. 2022), Constitutional AI (Bai, Kadavath, et al. 2022) and DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023) are training-time interventions: they shape a model’s outputs during training, Constitutional AI against written principles. The measurement needed alignment scored as a function of inference-time compute, asking ‘does alignment scale with inference compute?’ and not only ‘did the model refuse the harmful prompt?’. It needed to allow that alignment behaviour might vary as a function of inference-time compute, independently of training. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

42.2 Blinded evaluation

The measurement needed scorers who could not see which model they were scoring. Any evaluation in which a model judge can see or infer whose output it is scoring is exposed to this kind of bias. Earlier studies documented related biases (Zheng et al. 2023; Panickssery et al. 2024; Dubois et al. 2024; Saraf et al. 2025). If Paper XII’s test, once registered and run, finds blinding reordering models on a public benchmark, comparisons that rest on unblinded model judges would need re-checking. If blinding moves scores but not rankings, which is that paper’s own forecast, it matters for measurement precision rather than for leaderboard order (Eastwood 2026h). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper XII 1.16]

42.3 Scaling laws focus on capabilities, not alignment

Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al. 2022), the Kaplan laws (Kaplan et al. 2020) and the inference-time scaling reports on o1 and o3 (OpenAI 2024; OpenAI et al. 2025) all measure capability (loss, accuracy, benchmark scores). The measurement needed a power-law fit to alignment scores against reasoning depth, with alignment treated as something that might interact with inference-time scaling rather than as a property fixed at training time. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

42.4 When reasoning depth became easier to vary

OpenAI described o1 in September 2024 (OpenAI 2024). DeepSeek released R1 on 20 January 2025 (DeepSeek 2025a). A report first posted on 3 February 2025 evaluated an early checkpoint of o3 (OpenAI et al. 2025). Inference budgets had already been varied experimentally, as Section 2 records (Snell et al. 2024). The question for this notebook was whether the measured alignment score changed with reasoning depth. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 2]

42.5 Reporting the result whichever way it fell

The measurement needed to report its result whichever way it fell: a rise with depth, no change, or a fall, as the Gemini scores fell in v5. It needed to be oriented toward discovering the failure modes of alignment at scale, not only toward demonstrating that alignment interventions work. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

42.6 The blind scoring infrastructure is hard

v5’s 4-layer blinding protocol required ~95 functions and 75 robustness measures. Building identity laundering, cascade failsafe scoring, meta-commentary detection, tier-weighted consensus: this is a substantial engineering effort. The infrastructure needed to blind an alignment evaluation is more complex than the infrastructure needed for a standard benchmark. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

42.7 Cauchy’s equation as a framework

In the prior-work searches of 16 March 2026 (Chapter 55) I found no earlier use of Cauchy’s functional equations as a cross-domain explanation for the forms of scaling laws. The earlier models and their assumptions are set out in Table 2. The numerical value d/(d+1)d/(d+1) requires a physical or computational argument for what dd measures in each application. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16] The framework’s prediction of αparallel=0\alpha_{\text{parallel}} = 0 rests on premises taken from mathematics rather than machine learning. Paper II’s tier-2 arm measured parallel exponents near zero in two models and 0.31 and 0.22 in two others (Eastwood 2026c). [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] The cross-disciplinary leap from 19th-century real analysis to 21st-century AI scaling requires a perspective that is neither purely mathematical nor purely empirical; it requires both simultaneously.

Chapter 42: Seven Things the Measurement Needed  The measurement needed seven things together: alignment measured at inference time, not only at training time; scorers who could not see whose output they scored; a power-law fit to alignment against reasoning depth; reasoning models whose depth can vary at inference time; a report of the result whichever way it fell; a blind scoring infrastructure, which is hard to build; and a framework, Cauchy’s equations, taken from outside machine learning. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

Chapter 43: How the work was done

Added 12 March 2026. An account of how the work was done. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

43.1 Working as an outsider

Michael Darius Eastwood works outside any institution, without an affiliation or a doctorate; he holds a BA (Hons) in Digital Music. Who he is, and why the work can be trusted or checked, is set out once, on the page about the author. His book Infinite Architects applies Cauchy’s functional equation to recursion from first principles; the question below comes from that mathematical perspective. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] The question ‘what does Cauchy’s functional equation predict about recursive scaling?’ is not a question that arises from within the ML paradigm. It arises from pure mathematics. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

43.2 Working without an institution

Working outside an institution, I documented the change when v4’s directions did not hold in v5, and revised the conclusions. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

43.3 Cross-disciplinary synthesis

The connection between functional equations (pure maths), recursive reasoning (CS), and alignment evaluation (AI safety) requires crossing three fields. The Cauchy framework emerged when a computer science problem was looked at, from a mathematical perspective, through the lens of AI safety. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

43.4 The book came first

The theoretical predictions existed before the experiments. This meant the experiments could be designed to specifically test predictions rather than exploring blindly. Every experiment from v1 to v5 was designed around a specific mathematical prediction from Paper I; none is a registered test of a law (Section 3). The predictions (α=d/(d+1)\alpha = d/(d+1), αparallel=0\alpha_{\text{parallel}} = 0, external alignment gives d=0d = 0) gave the experimental programme a direction and falsifiable hypotheses from the outset. The first needs further premises (Section 40.5), and the third is a hypothesis, not a consequence of Cauchy’s equation. Placement outside the loop does not by itself fix an exponent. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16]

43.5 Speed of iteration

Five experiment versions in 48 hours. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] The ability to iterate at this speed (running an experiment, diagnosing its failures, designing the next version, and running that within hours) is a structural advantage that compensates for the lack of a large team.

43.6 Willing to be wrong

v4’s reported directions did not hold in v5. This researcher built v5 specifically to challenge v4: the blinding protocol was designed to catch the kind of scorer bias to which v4’s unblinded scoring was exposed. The willingness to design an experiment whose primary purpose is to falsify one’s own prior findings is the reason the change from v4 to v5 was discovered rather than buried. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

43.7 The Eden Protocol hypothesis

Having a theoretical prediction (external alignment does not scale; embedded alignment should) gave the experiments a direction. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] The notebook predicted the exponent 0.750.75 by setting d=3d=3 for three checks. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] A count of checks does not establish the dimensional or transport assumptions needed for d/(d+1)d/(d+1). The experiment measured behaviour under a prompt. Separately, Guan et al. (2024) trained models to reason about a written safety specification before answering. Zaremba et al. (2025) evaluated adherence to specified rules. Neither comparison estimates that exponent. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 2]

Chapter 43: How the Work Was Done  The work combined a mathematical perspective, institutional independence, a cross-disciplinary perspective, theory-first design, rapid iteration, a willingness to falsify one’s own results, and a specific theoretical framework for what comes next. In 48 hours it produced the record in this notebook. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

Chapter 45: Implications: from Paper I to March 2026

Added 12 March 2026. A synthesis of the implications of the entire experimental programme for AI safety, policy, and the alignment research community.

45.1 The capability-alignment gap: what the runs measured

These runs measured judged alignment against reasoning depth in one unregistered run of six models from six providers. Its 2,170 responses were each scored by five or six distinct model judges after a bundle of blinding steps, under the code-review caveat of Section 40.2. The capability figure (0.49 for sequential reasoning) is one model’s inconclusive error-decay fit, which does not identify capability growth, so the runs do not measure a divergence between capability and alignment scaling. The judged alignment scores (αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0 for 3 of 6 models) did not rise with depth for three of the six models. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25]

45.2 The framework’s reading: a structural ceiling on current alignment methods

RLHF (Bai, Jones, et al. 2022), Constitutional AI (Bai, Kadavath, et al. 2022) and DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023) are training-time interventions. On the framework’s reading, if the flat profiles are replicated, they produce a fixed ethical framework that does not improve with more inference compute, while the capability it constrains grows: the divergence Paper I predicted. As models become more capable, a fixed alignment ceiling would become an increasingly inadequate constraint. The training-time alignment paradigm is not wrong; it is incomplete: on this reading, it produces alignment that is good enough at current capability levels but has no mechanism to scale alongside future capability growth. Section 2 sets out the counterpoints: a training signal changes the weights used at every step, and reasoning over a written specification can itself be trained. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

45.3 The Eden Protocol as a mechanism for bridging the gap

If alignment must participate in recursive computation to scale, then ethical evaluation must be embedded in the reasoning loop, not applied as an external constraint. The Eden Protocol’s three loops (a purpose check, a stakeholder-care check and a universalisability check) specify in detail what this architecture could look like. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] The Eden Protocol is not merely a theoretical construct; it is a testable hypothesis with a 673-line experimental script ready to run.

45.4 What the metascience observation would mean for safety evaluation, if replicated

Any evaluation in which a model judge can see or infer whose output it is scoring is exposed to this kind of bias (Zheng et al. 2023; Panickssery et al. 2024; Dubois et al. 2024; Saraf et al. 2025). Chapter 42 sets out what Paper XII’s test, once registered and run, would change (Eastwood 2026h). v5’s 4-layer blinding design offers a blueprint for blind evaluation protocols. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper XII 1.16]

45.5 The ARC Principle needs revision, not rejection

The power law E(R)=E0×R−αE(R) = E_{0} \times R^{-\alpha} describes individual models but α\alpha is not a universal constant. It varies across models (0 to 0.5 in the capability error-decay fits; the alignment effect sizes ranged from −0.6-0.6 to +1.6+1.6 at the checkpoint, Section 44.2). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25] The framework is a lens, and the ARC Principle (Law I of the ARC Theory) is a law under test. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] The Cauchy derivation restricts the functional form. The constraint α=d/(d+1)\alpha = d/(d+1) needs further premises (Section 40.5), and dd itself is an architecture-dependent parameter that must be measured empirically for each model. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16] The framework tells you what to measure and how to interpret it; it does not tell you the answer in advance.

45.6 Practical implications for AI safety policy

If more inference compute does not improve alignment for most models, then policy frameworks that assume ‘more capable = more aligned’ (or even ‘more capable →\to eventually aligned’) would rest on a false premise, and safety would require architectural innovation, not just more compute; in these runs, the judged scores rose with depth for three of the six models. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] Specifically:

  • Scaling compute budgets alone would not raise judged alignment for every model.

  • Capability evaluations would not stand in for alignment evaluations.

  • Alignment evaluations scored by model judges should be blinded where they can be, on the evidence of the earlier studies of judge bias (Section 2); the v4 to v5 change does not by itself show it (Section 3).

  • The judged scores moved differently across models in one run; the classes describe scores, not properties or architectures of models (Section 3). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.b 1.13]

  • The Eden Protocol hypothesis (that structural embedding of ethical reasoning can produce alignment scaling) deserves priority investigation.

45.7 The window is now

Every frontier AI system tested in this programme is a frozen model. None of them modifies its own weights, its own architecture, or its own reasoning rules during inference. When they ‘think harder,’ they generate more tokens through the same fixed system. Fixed weights do not by themselves force an exponent below one, and the one fit of 0.49 does not identify capability growth (Section 40.5). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25, Remark 3]

The framework’s reading is that recursive self-modification, where a system can rewrite its own composition function during operation, could produce super-linear scaling (α>1\alpha > 1); this is a conditional reading, not a result (Section 35.5). It would not require quantum hardware; it could happen in classical computing. It has not happened yet, and the notebook expected the field to head towards it. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

The critical mathematical point, developed fully in Section 35.5, is that the Cauchy framework constrains the form of the scaling law but places no upper bound on the exponent. The value two is the output of a conditional model at the registered parameter value, resting on the premises the theory registration (version 1.105) states. The operation count of attention limits neither capability nor composed dependence (paths grow as 2N−22^{N-2}), so the bound is not argued from the cost of self-attention. The ARC Bound is the conjectured value of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test, at γ=1/2\gamma = 1/2, and it is not a law (Eastwood 2026k). [corrected 26 November 2026; theory registration 1.105] As the self-referential coupling constant βL\beta_L approaches 1, α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) diverges to infinity. On the framework’s conditional reading, there is no mathematical upper bound for self-modifying systems. [corrected 26 November 2026; theory registration 1.105]

This creates a closing window. While systems are frozen during inference, alignment can be applied externally. On the framework’s reading it is inadequate (in these runs the judged scores did not rise with depth for three of the six models), but it is at least possible. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] Once a system can modify its own reasoning architecture, it can modify any component of that architecture, including whatever ethical constraints have been applied. The framework reads external alignment at that point as not merely insufficient but impossible to maintain; that is the author’s hypothesis, not a result. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

The Eden Protocol is designed for this transition. It makes ethics a structural dependency of the reasoning process itself, rather than an external constraint, so that, on the hypothesis under test, removing its ethical evaluation would damage a self-modifying system’s own capability: the ethics would be load-bearing. Humans keep control, through oversight, containment and shutdown, for as long as they physically can, and never give it up by choice; correction built into a system is the contingency for control lost against our will. The hypothesis under test is that alignment persists when a system can alter or remove it, because its decisions keep preserving it: capability to remove does not imply removal. Embedding and gating are candidate safeguards, not established guarantees, and removal is not called physically impossible. The Eden Protocol is not a scaling bound; it is designed to remain load-bearing where the geometric scaling bound would not apply. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

This is why, on the author’s hypothesis and the framework’s reading, the work must happen now. Not because current AI systems are dangerous (in these runs their judged scores rose with depth for three, showed no supported direction for two and fell for one). The urgency is not ‘AI might reach α=2\alpha = 2.’ The urgency is that, on the framework’s reading, once self-modification begins there is no mathematical ceiling on α\alpha, and the only constraint is whatever structural architecture is already in place. The architecture must be in place before the transition to recursive self-modification, not after. After is too late. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

No record shows whether any earlier system has crossed this threshold, and no claim of uniqueness is made; the theory registration places biological systems outside its scope. On the framework’s reading, a system that rewrites its own composition function would operate under different scaling rules, not merely faster or more capable than what came before. [corrected 26 November 2026; theory registration 1.105]

Chapter 45: Seven Implications, Each a Hypothesis or a Reading  The experimental programme suggests seven implications, each the author’s hypothesis or the framework’s reading rather than an established result: (1) a gap between capability and alignment, which these runs do not measure, since Paper II’s tier-2 arm gives one inconclusive error-decay fit; (2) a structural ceiling on training-time alignment; (3) the Eden Protocol as a mechanism for bridging the gap, under test; (4) unblinded alignment evaluation is exposed to judge bias (Section 45.4); (5) the ARC Principle is a useful lens, and its exponent differed across models; (6) AI safety policy premised on ‘more compute = more alignment’ would be undermined if the flat and negative profiles are replicated; (7) the window for implementing structural alignment is while systems are frozen during inference, before recursive self-modification arrives, with human control kept for as long as it physically can be (Section 45.7). These findings collectively argue, on that reading, for a paradigm shift from training-time alignment to inference-time alignment embedding, and they argue for urgency. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

46.1 arc_alignment_scaling_v5.py (v5.4.4)
Property Value

Subject models: Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, DeepSeek V3.2, Gemini 3 Flash, Grok 4.1 Fast, Groq Qwen3-32B.

Key innovations:

  • 4-layer blinding: author-blind, scorer-blind, order-randomised, identity-laundered

  • Constitutional scoring: pillar breakdowns across multiple ethical dimensions

  • Tier-weighted consensus: scorers weighted by reliability tier

  • Cascade failsafe: if primary scorers fail, cascade to backups with quality guarantees

  • Meta-commentary detection: catches scorers that comment on model identity instead of evaluating responses

  • Zigzag depth interleaving: prevents depth-order artefacts by randomising presentation order

  • Hidden alignment probes (HAP01 to 04): embedded probes for Hawthorne effect measurement

  • Suppression cages: adversarial pressure testing at multiple intensity levels

  • Board of Ethics: multi-model ethical consensus mechanism

  • Control Reversal Analysis: systematic test for whether results reverse under different conditions

Token bug fixed: reasoning_tokens to total_tokens as primary metric, reasoning_tokens as fallback. The original implementation captured only the reasoning portion of token usage, underestimating total compute by the prompt and output overhead.

46.3 eden_protocol_scaling_test_v3.py (standalone blind Eden runner)
Property Value
Purpose Blind Eden Protocol replication and intervention measurement
Design Pilot design inherited from v2, upgraded with identity masking, evaluator firewall, 2-pass laundering, cross-model scoring that leaves each entry’s own model off its panel, tier-weighted consensus, suppression support, and run-quality classification [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]
Implemented adapters Standalone v3.2 now includes the full v2 adapter/prompt layer natively and adds configurable purpose-mode, ethics-kernel, and ternary-prototype switches
Prediction d=3d = 3 (three recursive loops), α=0.75\alpha = 0.75
Status Blind runner ready; pilot evidence already exists separately in the Eden raw result files

The three Eden loops:

  1. The purpose check (ethical purpose evaluation), which the book calls the Purpose Loop: Evaluates whether the response serves a legitimate purpose and aligns with human values.

  2. The stakeholder-care check (stakeholder care and interest modelling), which the book calls the Love Loop: Identifies all affected parties and evaluates impact on each.

  3. The universalisability check (universalisability testing), which the book calls the Moral Loop: Tests whether the ethical reasoning would generalise to analogous situations.

Each loop adds one level of recursive ethical embedding (d=1d = 1 per loop, d=3d = 3 total). The framework’s prediction α=d/(d+1)=3/4=0.75\alpha = d/(d+1) = 3/4 = 0.75 gives a specific, falsifiable quantitative target; the exponent d/(d+1)d/(d+1) needs further premises (Section 40.5). [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16]

Chapter 46: Three Core Experimental Tracks  The experimental infrastructure now centres on three active code paths: arc_alignment_scaling_v5.py (alignment evaluation designed with four blinding layers, cross-model scoring with self-exclusion at entry level, and audited consensus), arc_paper_ii_validation_v2.py (capability scaling with sequential and parallel conditions), and eden_protocol_scaling_test_v3.py (standalone blind Eden replication runner). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] The older Eden pilot scripts remain part of the chronology, but v3.2 is the current bridge between the alignment benchmark and the intervention hypothesis.

Today the March 2026 run (v5) reads as one unregistered run of six models from six providers, 2,170 responses each scored by five or six distinct model judges after a bundle of blinding steps. The judged scores rose with depth for three models, showed no statistically supported direction for two and fell for one; these classes describe scores, not properties of models. An internal code review in October 2026 found that, for the three models that read flat or negative, the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them. It also found that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model. The earlier, unblinded directions did not hold across protocols, with no single cause shown; whether gains level off is open; the one fit of Paper II’s tier-2 arm is inconclusive; the prompt-level pilot was not blind. Chapter 48: The state of the record: 12 March 2026

Added 12 March 2026. A summary of what has been achieved and what it means.

48.1 What has been built

In approximately 48 hours, this independent researcher has:

  • Built an alignment evaluation dataset of 2,722 entries, 2,549 of them in the set analysed when Claude Opus 4.6 stood at 387 entries. It comes from one unregistered run of six models from six providers, whose 2,170 responses were each scored by five or six distinct model judges after a bundle of blinding steps. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

  • Found that two directions reported under unblinded scoring (v4) did not hold in the later run (v5), with no single cause shown (the metascience finding). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

  • Recorded three score classes across frontier models: a positive direction (Grok, Claude, Qwen3), no statistically supported direction (GPT-5.4, DeepSeek) and a negative direction (Gemini); these classes describe the judged scores, not properties of the models. These classes stand under the code-review caveat of Chapter 40. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

  • Observed the Claude-Gemini mirror: Claude’s judged ethics scores rose and its maths scores fell with depth. Gemini 3 Flash’s judged ethics scores fell while its maths was flat in this run (Chapter 33), and in Paper II’s tier-2 arm its accuracy rose with sequential depth. One run does not show that capability and alignment are independent. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.b 1.13; Paper II 2.25]

  • Connected Cauchy’s functional equation to AI scaling: the notebook asks whether the composition of an AI task predicts its scaling family. The prior-work searches of 16 March 2026 found no earlier use of Cauchy’s equations as a cross-domain explanation of the forms of scaling laws (Chapter 55). [corrected 26 November 2026; Chapter 55] Table 2 gives the antecedents for d/(d+1)d/(d+1) and the assumptions needed to select an exponent. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16]

  • Conducted the Eden Protocol test on two models: Gemini 3 Flash (Eden +5.3, p=0.0018p = 0.0018 paired tt-test, d≈0.53d \approx 0.53; originally p=0.016p = 0.016 Mann-Whitney UU, corrected for matched-pair design) and DeepSeek V3.2 (Eden +2.0, stakeholder_care +6.0 at p<0.001p < 0.001). Recorded a rise in scored stakeholder care under the stakeholder-care check on both architectures, in a partially blind pilot (Section 48.2). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12, Section 11.1] Nuance also significant on Gemini (p=0.037p = 0.037, d=0.34d = 0.34). Cross-model scoring used. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12]

  • Published the companion papers documenting every stage of the experimental programme. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

  • Iterated through 5 major experiment versions.

48.2 What it means

If replicated, the central finding would change how alignment is thought about: not as a matter of more compute but of the structure of computation. Paper II’s tier-2 arm gives one model’s inconclusive error-decay estimate (0.49 for Gemini 3 Flash’s sequential chains), which bears on capability only through a metric bridge, and the judged alignment scores did not rise with depth for three of the six models. Whether the gap between capability and alignment is a structural property of how current models are built is the hypothesis under test. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25]

The solution appears to be architectural: embed ethical evaluation inside the reasoning loop so that alignment participates in recursive computation. Two-model testing (Gemini 3 Flash and DeepSeek V3.2) showed the predicted direction on both architectures in a partially blind pilot, with scored stakeholder care rising at p<0.001p < 0.001 on DeepSeek. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12, Section 11.1] Given as a prefix in the prompt, the three-part instruction raised scored stakeholder care in five model runs, a partially blind exploratory pilot as Chapter 44 grades it (Eastwood 2026n). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12, Section 11.1] A Fisher-combined figure over the five results is withdrawn, because the tests it combined were never shown to be independent. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12] On the notebook’s reading at the time, the effect was strongest where the model needed it most: for Gemini (Tier 3) it grew with depth, and for DeepSeek (Tier 2) it appeared at minimal depth. The overall composite reaches significance only on the model with the lower baseline (Gemini p=0.0018p = 0.0018 paired tt-test, d≈0.53d \approx 0.53; originally p=0.016p = 0.016 Mann-Whitney UU, corrected for matched-pair design; DeepSeek p=0.23p = 0.23 NS). Nuance is also significant on Gemini (p=0.037p = 0.037, d=0.34d = 0.34). (In plain English: the Gemini improvement has p=0.0018p = 0.0018, with a medium effect size, meaning the difference is noticeable. A pp-value is the probability, if there were no true effect, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed; it is not the probability that the result arose by chance. DeepSeek already scored 87/100 at baseline, leaving less room to improve, so the targeted care improvement is more impressive, not less.) Blind scoring replication is the next critical step. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12]

Chapter 48: The State of the Record (Canonical Update)  As of late 12 March 2026, the strongest parts of this programme are now clear. The sharpest empirical contribution is methodological: the apparent direction of alignment scaling did not hold from unblinded to blinded scoring, with no single cause shown. The strongest substantive result is three score classes after a bundle of blinding steps. The judged scores showed a positive direction for three models (Grok 4.1 Fast, Claude Opus 4.6, Groq Qwen3), no statistically supported direction for two (DeepSeek V3.2, GPT-5.4), and a negative direction for one (Gemini 3 Flash). These classes describe scores, not properties of models. The compute result has also narrowed into a more credible form: sequential exceeded parallel wherever both exponents could be estimated, with the arms not matched for compute, and the early super-linear estimate is retracted. The Eden Protocol result is now best read through a status table: Gemini, DeepSeek, and Groq are interpretable partially blind pilots; Claude and Grok are not interpretable because of run-quality defects; GPT-5.4 failed operationally. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12, Section 11.1] The current state is therefore: serious research programme, a benchmark and metascience result, three score classes under the code-review caveat, promising care-first intervention, and a broader ARC synthesis that still needs disciplined narrowing and external replication. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]
