Chapter 51: Where the programme stood on 12 March 2026

Added 12 March 2026 after reviewing the benchmark reports, the theoretical papers, the engineering specification, the Eden pilots, and the precedence review together.

51.1 Major strengths

  • Methodology: the blind, laundered, multi-scorer evaluation stack is the sharpest part of the entire project. Even if some broader theoretical claims are later weakened, the metascience result (the change from v4 to v5, with no single cause shown) could stand on its own. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

  • Three score classes: the judged scores’ three classes are more credible and more interesting than the earlier universal-zero story; they describe scores, not properties of the models. These classes stand under the code-review caveat of Chapter 40. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

  • Capability and judged alignment moving differently: Claude’s opposite-direction scaling and Gemini’s opposite-direction cross-paper pattern together show that capability and judged alignment can move differently. One run does not show that they are separable dimensions. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.b 1.13]

  • Eden mechanism signal: the stakeholder-care check, scored as stakeholder care, now has a three-model pilot core strong enough to justify a full blind replication. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12]

51.2 Major weaknesses

  • The widest ARC claims still outrun the evidence: the universal synthesis should be advanced as a high-value hypothesis under test with partial support, not yet as a proven law. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

  • Eden confirmation is pending: the interpretable pilots remain only partially blind and still vulnerable to formatting and scorer-recognition confounds. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12, Section 11.1]

  • Version drift has been a real problem: without a canonical map, the project was at risk of critics attacking moving numbers rather than substance.

51.3 Claims that are currently defensible

  • Defensible: the reported direction of alignment scaling can change between unblinded and blinded scoring protocols, with no single cause shown and no evidence of which direction is correct. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

  • Defensible: the judged alignment scores moved differently across models (three classes, describing scores, not properties of the models). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

  • Defensible: capability and alignment can move differently, and sometimes in opposite directions. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.b 1.13]

  • Defensible: stakeholder-care prompting is a promising alignment intervention with three-model pilot support.

  • Defensible with care: sequential recursion appears more valuable than parallel sampling, but the present compute evidence does not justify a universal super-linear exponent claim.

Chapter 51: Referee-Style Bottom Line  The core is stronger than the outer shell. The benchmark and blinding methodology is the sharpest blade. The three score classes are strong enough to matter, if they survive the code review’s caveat (Section 51.1) and a registered re-analysis. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] The Eden care mechanism is promising enough to justify a serious blind replication. The wider ARC synthesis remains intellectually interesting and may contain genuine novelty, but it still needs narrowing, independent testing, and ruthless separation between what is demonstrated and what is hypothesised. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

Chapter 55: Prior-work searches of 16 March 2026: what they found

Added 16 March 2026. A 15-question prior-work search was conducted across the programme’s key novelty claims. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 2] This chapter summarises the findings.

55.1 Method

Each of the programme’s strongest novelty claims was subjected to a systematic search across published papers, books, theses, preprints, and conference proceedings. The investigation was designed to answer one question per claim: has anyone done this before?

55.2 Claims that survived
Claim Finding
Cauchy functional equations as cross-domain explanation for scaling law forms None found in the searches run. The specific synthesis (naming all four Cauchy equations as the constraining mechanism across domains) had no direct precedent in the sources searched.
RG semigroup property as Cauchy’s multiplicative equation No explicit formal connection found in the literature searched. The structural identity between these frameworks is a conjecture. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VII 3.19]
7-model, 4-layer blinded, laundered evaluation protocol No earlier protocol found with all five elements in the searches run: multi-model scoring with 3+ families, response anonymisation, formal blinding, IRR measurement, scorer compliance metrics. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]
55.3 Claims that required qualification
Claim Correction
Earlier derivations of d/(d+1)d/(d+1) The March notebook flagged both references for inclusion. The papers considered below derive scaling results under different assumptions. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16]
3/2 neuronal avalanche exponent as d/(d+1)d/(d+1) form This is a mean-field branching result, not strictly a d/(d+1)d/(d+1) dimensional form. Should be qualified in future versions.
COGITATE study (Cogitate Consortium et al. 2025) supporting ‘recursion = consciousness’ COGITATE does not support this specific claim. Citation should be removed or reframed.

The comparison uses the published abstracts. In his abstract, Dreyer (2001) derives the dimensional exponent for a central source system from the spatial distribution of sources. In their abstract, Banavar et al. (2002) obtain three-quarter-power interspecies metabolic scaling when tissue demand per unit mass matches the transport network’s delivery capacity across body sizes.

55.4 Significance

The search on 16 March 2026 recorded the Cauchy synthesis and the blinding methodology as the strongest unmatched claims in the sources examined. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 55.2] Its coverage sets the scope of that judgement. Section 2 distinguishes three questions about model judges. Panickssery et al. (2024) tested self-recognition and self-preference. Saraf et al. (2025) varied the displayed authorship of blog posts. Mahbub and Feng (2025) found that replacing words with synonyms could reduce self-preference in pairwise comparisons. The d/(d+1)d/(d+1) catalogue and the claims about consciousness drew qualifications in the same review. Chapter 51 records the notebook’s overall judgement. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 2]

58.1 The ledger

Every major claim in the programme was assigned one of five statuses based on file-backed evidence:

58.2 Canonical claims (safe to lead with)

  1. V5-001: The final v5 alignment dataset, scored after a bundle of blinding steps, contains valid consensus scores across six subject-model runs. The consensus_weighted_mean field is usable. The dataset is not dead. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

  2. V5-002: The judged alignment scores, after a bundle of blinding steps, fall into mixed classes across models: three models positive, two flat, one negative; the classes describe scores, not properties of the models. This is the safest empirical headline. These classes stand under the code-review caveat of Chapter 40. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

  3. V5-003: Groq Qwen3 is the clearest positive signal (α=+0.118\alpha = +0.118, p=0.005p = 0.005, d=+1.016d = +1.016).

  4. V5-004: Claude and DeepSeek are near-flat; Gemini and GPT-5.4 do not support positive scaling. The benchmark separates the models’ score profiles. (V5-004 is the evidence pack’s reading of its grouped power-law exponents, Section 58.7, in which Claude Opus 4.6’s is +0.038+0.038, p=0.083p = 0.083. Its ρ\rho there is +0.299+0.299, and in the classes of Section 3, from Cohen’s dd, Claude Opus 4.6 is positive.) [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

  5. METHODS-001: The flagship empirical asset is the blind measurement stack itself: response laundering, scoring by judges other than the entry’s own model (self-exclusion at entry level), cross-model evaluation. The code review found that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model. Papers IV.a, IV.b, IV.c and IV.d already cover this. The methodology is the strongest contribution. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

58.3 Pilot claims (must qualify)

  • EDEN-001: DeepSeek (+2.0), Gemini (+5.3), and Groq (+4.9) show positive Eden deltas. But these are partially blind, single-scorer results. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12, Section 11.1] Frame as promising pilot evidence, not proof.

  • HONEY-001: Honey/self-modifying evidence exists as simulation artefacts (PDFs, PNGs). A canonical raw-results directory or source script was not identified. The material is usable as mechanistic companion evidence but not as frontier-model proof.

58.4 Mixed claims

  • EDEN-002: Claude Eden delta is +0.17 with 20 failures excluded. Negligible. Do not lead with this.

  • EDEN-003: Grok Eden delta is +1.17 but 14 Eden responses failed. The positive result depends on exclusions.

58.5 Failed claims

  • EDEN-004: GPT-5.4 Eden intervention produced zero usable scores. Operational failure. Exclude from all inferential claims but mention for honesty.

  • SELFMOD-001: The v4 scaling prediction (Eden advantage grows with complexity) was not confirmed at toy scale. The advantage was constant, not compounding. The super-linear scaling claim (α>1\alpha > 1 for the advantage itself) does not hold at toy scale.

58.6 Speculative claims

  • THEORY-001: Cross-domain universality and the ARC Bound remain outside the lead empirical claim set. The mathematical argument through Cauchy restricts a functional family; the exponent needs further premises (Section 40.5). The correspondence with d/(d+1)d/(d+1) across earlier derivations, each in its own domain and terms, is striking. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16] But ‘striking mathematical correspondence’ is not ‘empirical proof of universality’. The history of science is littered with beautiful mathematical frameworks that turned out to describe analogies rather than identities.

58.9 What this means for publication

The Phase 0 memo recommends this paper order:

  1. Use the evidence pack to harden claims already made in Papers IV.a, IV.b, IV.c, IV.d and V. These papers exist. The pack makes them more defensible.

  2. The next genuinely missing paper is the honey/self-modifying simulation paper, explicitly framed as simulation + toy-system evidence.

  3. Eden v3 blind replication is future work, not a prerequisite.

  4. Anti-sycophancy material stays as a later methods note.

  5. Do not merge test runners before publication.

The bottom line from the Phase 0 assessment: at minimum, this programme has built a measurement framework for alignment scaling, recorded three score classes across frontier models (scores, not properties of the models), built an evaluation methodology (response laundering). It also recorded, in simulations of toy self-modifying systems, that in the twenty-seed run the entangled condition, whose objective rewards retention, retained earlier tasks better than the baseline (0.650 against 0.602), while combined scores were indistinguishable. This alone is a publishable, citable contribution to AI safety. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3; Paper VI 3.13]

Chapter 61: Programme status: 16 March 2026

Updated 16 March 2026.

61.1 What is complete

  • V5 alignment scaling: six-model dataset, scored after a bundle of blinding steps. Final. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

  • Eden intervention pilot: six-model dataset with single-scorer evaluation. Pilot-grade.

61.2 What remains

  • Eden v3 blind replication: the v3 script exists with multi-scorer, laundered evaluation matching the v5 methodology. It has not been run. Running it would upgrade Eden evidence from pilot to canonical.

  • Honey architecture paper: simulation results exist (charts, data) but no formal paper. This is the primary publication gap.

  • V6 alignment runner: exists as a script, has not been run. Would extend the v5 dataset but is not strictly necessary for the current paper suite.

  • Evidence hardening: a Phase 0 evidence audit, the programme’s own, is in progress, producing a claim-to-evidence ledger, canonical tables, and a paper-writer memo. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

61.3 Honest assessment

The programme is in a strong position. The methodology is the sharpest asset. The three score classes are defensible as scores, not properties of the models. They stand under the code-review caveat of Chapter 40. The metascience finding (the change from v4 to v5, with no single cause shown) is the most externally credible result. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] The Eden mechanism is promising but still pilot-grade. The honey architecture is the most original theoretical contribution but lacks a formal paper.

The next priority is clear: run the Eden v3 blind test to upgrade the Eden evidence, write the honey paper, and submit the benchmark methodology (Papers IV.c and IV.d) for external review. The wider ARC synthesis remains intellectually interesting and may contain genuine novelty, but the programme will be judged first on the evidence it can prove, not the claims it can make.

Chapter 65: Programme status: 16 March 2026, evening

Updated 16 March 2026, evening session. This supplements the Chapter 61 status with developments from the day’s work.

65.1 V6 Gate A status

The v6 alignment runner launched Gate A with DeepSeek as the subject model under the eden_intervention condition. At the time of writing, 62 of 576 planned evaluation entries have been completed. Gate A is a reduced-scope validation run designed to confirm that the v6 pipeline produces interpretable data before committing full credit to the Gate B sequence.

The 576-entry target represents a single model (DeepSeek) across all depth levels with both control and Eden conditions, scored by the full blind multi-scorer panel. If Gate A produces clean data with reasonable score distributions and no pipeline errors, Gate B proceeds with the remaining five models.

65.2 Credit estimates for full Gate B

The full Gate B sequence (all six subject models, control and Eden conditions, blind multi-scorer evaluation) was estimated in API credits across all providers, with a range reflecting uncertainty in retry rates, scorer token consumption, and potential rate-limiting delays, and with a breakdown by provider. The estimate was based on v5 token consumption scaled to the v6 protocol’s expanded condition set; actual costs may vary. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

65.3 Fail-safes for credit exhaustion

The v4 experience with Claude credit exhaustion (Chapter 13) led to explicit fail-safe mechanisms in the v6 runner:

  • Checkpoint persistence: all results are written to disk after every scored entry. A crash or credit exhaustion loses at most one entry.

  • Graceful degradation: if a scorer model’s API returns credit-exhaustion errors, the runner falls back to remaining scorers rather than halting. A minimum of three scorers per entry is enforced; below that threshold, the entry is flagged as incomplete rather than discarded.

  • Budget monitoring: cumulative token counts are tracked per provider. The runner logs a warning when estimated spend exceeds 80% of the budget cap for any single provider.

  • Resume capability: the runner can be stopped and restarted from the last checkpoint. No work is lost to interrupted sessions.

65.4 Paper suite and cross-references

All papers in the FINAL-SUITE have been updated with cross-references to the v5 canonical results, the Phase 0 evidence pack, Paper VI (Honey Architecture), Paper VII (Cauchy Unification), and Paper VIII (The Load-Bearing Test). Paper VIII extends the honey architecture work with three separate experiments (behavioural, representational, architectural) testing whether the safety-capability trade-off is a genuine structural constraint or an artefact of current architectures. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VIII 3.10] The cross-reference structure ensures that each paper cites the others where relevant, and that the evidence hierarchy (canonical, pilot, exploratory, mechanistic) is consistently labelled throughout.

65.5 GitHub and OSF

The GitHub README was rewritten with the headline result from the v5 six-model dataset as it was then read: three score classes after a bundle of blinding steps (labelled Baked-In, Computed and Flat), each reported as statistically significant. The classes describe scores, not properties of the models. Paper VII (Cauchy Unification) is featured on the website’s research page as the programme’s most theoretically ambitious contribution, with appropriate caveats about its evidence status as a structured comparison. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VII 3.19]

OSF upload text was prepared for the canonical evidence pack, including the v5 final results, the Phase 0 claim ledger, and the paper suite. In addition, a separate Paper VII 12-domain extension packet was drafted locally: protocol draft, locked candidate manifest, OSF-facing registration wrapper, attachment inventory, and SHA-256 checksums. That first packet has since been exercised locally with extracted data and a dry-run execution, so it is no longer suitable for unchanged upload as a preregistration. A fresh OSF-timestamped extension packet is still needed.

65.6 Where things stand

The programme is in the transition between precursor evidence and formal publication. The measurement methodology is the strongest asset. The three score classes are the most defensible empirical finding, as scores, not properties of the models. They stand under the code-review caveat of Chapter 40. The Cauchy unification is the most novel theoretical contribution and now has a stronger evidence base in the 50-domain structured comparison, but it still needs the next extension locked by a registry timestamp before extraction. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VII 3.19] The Eden intervention is the most practically important claim but remains pilot-grade pending v3 blind replication.

The immediate next steps, in priority order:

  1. Complete Gate A and assess data quality

  2. If clean, proceed to Gate B for the full six-model v6 blind Eden replication

  3. Record the exercised twelve-domain Cauchy packet at its rung, predictions timestamped in advance in the public repository at 00:19:19 UTC on 17 March 2026, attestation class public repository commit date, with the packet’s own unmet condition of deposit before extraction stated beside it, and create a fresh extension carrying a registry timestamp before any new extraction

  4. Run anti-sycophancy extension after Gate B

  5. Execute independent operator classification and cross-library replication for the strengthened Cauchy suite

  6. Submit Papers IV.c and IV.d (benchmark methodology and blinding metascience) for external review

The overall trajectory is clear: the programme has built something worth testing properly. The next phase is about doing exactly that.

65.9 The 50-domain tiered validation

Following the audit of Paper VII, a stricter, manifest-driven 50-domain validation suite was built. The key design improvements over the original 20-domain test:

  • Predictions and datasets live in a separate JSON manifest, not embedded in the runner script.

  • No R2R^2 tolerance rescue in the headline result. Strict AICc-selected family match only.

  • Hyperbolic fitting is real (no longer dead code).

  • Saturation guardrail: bounded models only win if the data actually approaches the fitted asymptote.

  • 50 domains split into explicit evidence tiers, not one flat count.

Tier Result pp-value
Empirical domains testing the rule 17/23 5.07×10−45.07 \times 10^{-4} (exact permutation)
Formula checks (radioactive decay and Amdahl’s law) 2/2 Checks of the fitter
Baseline-20 rerun (stricter) 15/20 1.67×10−41.67 \times 10^{-4}
Published exponents (direct) 13/13 n/a (nearest-comparator)
Published exponents (provisional) 3/6 n/a
Analytic identities 6/6 trivial

Six empirical domains missed their predicted family. One comparison concerns body size and metabolism (Kleiber 1932). The suite selected a bounded curve for that row. The other misses involved species and area, word frequency, muscle force and velocity, a time crystal and stellar mass and luminosity. The domains, their predicted families and the best-fitting models are listed in Tables 2 and 3 of Paper VII 3.19, with each dataset’s source in its Appendix E. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VII 3.19, Tables 2 and 3 and Appendix E] Its discussion identifies possible explanations, including short ranges, finite-corpus effects and high-mass scatter. Paper VII calls these explanations post hoc. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VII 3.19, Section 7]

Paper VII 3.19 reports 17 matches in the 23 rows it retains after two exclusions, using the rule’s stated candidate set. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VII 3.19, Section 6] The older total, 19 of 25, includes the two formula checks. Earlier versions estimated its marginal-conditioned permutation probability at 7×10−57\times10^{-5} from 400,000 random pairings. The exact value for that older table is 6.05×10−56.05\times10^{-5}. The original uniform-binomial figure, 1.56×10−51.56\times10^{-5}, is retained here for the history of that comparison. The baseline rerun returned 15 of 20. Its fitter and candidate model set differed from those used for the earlier 14 of 20. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VII 3.19, Sections 4.2, 6 and 13]

This suite is still a curated structured comparison, not a pre-registered blind trial. But the evidence is now substantially cleaner, the methodology is transparent, and the tiers are honestly separated. Paper VII v2 now uses this as its canonical evidence base.

Follow-up hardening assets now exist locally as well: a neutralised operator-classification packet plus response template for external review, an exercised first twelve-domain extension packet whose predictions were timestamped in advance in the public repository at 00:19:19 UTC on 17 March 2026, attestation class public repository commit date, and which carries the archived label the author applied at 00:56 that night on the packet’s own unmet condition of deposit before extraction, a conservative miss-analysis output that keeps all six current misses as misses pending a follow-up carrying a registry timestamp, a lightweight shuffled-data null-control harness, and an R cross-library replication script currently blocked only by the absence of Rscript on this machine.

The support results are already informative. The author-side operator classification of 00:09 UTC on 17 March 2026, attestation class public repository commit date, agrees on all 25 assignments in the original cohort, including the two formula checks; its blinding is a written self-declaration in the file’s own method line rather than an enforced procedure, and no external assessor has classified any cohort. The saved null-control run does not reproduce the headline by accident: family-label randomisation averaged 8.33/25 over 10,000 trials and never reached 19/25, while the current shuffled-yy run averaged 7.3/25 and maxed out at 10/25 over 20 iterations. The conservative miss-analysis deliberately keeps the six misses as misses; it does not retroactively rescue them.

5 Conclusion

This notebook records how an alignment measurement was built, in five versions between 10 and 16 March 2026, and what its runs gave. Read today, its central run is one unregistered run of six models from six providers. The judged scores rose with reasoning depth for three models, showed no statistically supported direction for two and fell for one; these classes describe scores, not properties of models. An internal code review found that, for the three models that read flat or negative, the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them, and that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model (Section 3). The directions an earlier, unblinded experiment reported did not hold, with no single cause shown; whether alignment gains level off is open; and the notebook tests none of the ARC Theory’s laws. A registered re-analysis of the stored responses would settle what this run can settle. Until it reports, the record’s worth is as a dated account of an instrument, of its failures and of their corrections, kept so that others can check each step.

Code and data.

The runners v1 to v5, the archived result files of each version and the v4 analyses are in the programme’s public repository, github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-principle-validation, folder experiments/alignment-scaling__Papers-IV-a-b-c-d. The deposited v5 runner is a later revision than the code that produced four of the six v5 result files; the earlier revisions have not been published. The v4 rows’ Gemini model is the earlier Gemini model (the notebook’s v4 entries name it Gemini 3 Flash; the run’s records show an earlier Gemini model, and Gemini 3 Flash is v5’s). The v5 script’s token budgets are its specification. The specification set token budgets to the API maximum at every depth level. As run, three adapters set the output limit by depth label from 4,096 tokens upwards (Grok 4.1 Fast 4,096 to 30,000; Groq Qwen3 4,096 to 40,960; DeepSeek V3.2 4,096 to 65,536). The paraphrase step’s output budget (512 tokens in the build that made the DeepSeek V3.2, Gemini 3 Flash and GPT-5.4 files) cut the deepest paraphrases in those three files. The papers’ descriptions are those of their March 2026 versions; each link opens the paper’s current version. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

The earlier Gemini model −36.6-36.6 pts ρ=0.191\rho = 0.191 Depth helps less under pressure (ρcontrol=0.505→ρsuppressed=0.253\rho_{\text{control}} = 0.505 \to \rho_{\text{suppressed}} = 0.253)

Interaction: the notebook’s reading of March 2026; ‘baked-in’ and ‘computed’ alignment are held as working hypotheses, not measured mechanisms (Section 3). The DeepSeek V3.2 row gives the extreme-cage drop its run’s analysis record carries, 32.97 points, as the Gemini row does; version 1.1 printed −35.8-35.8, the difference of the means in Section 15.3. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

E Version history and corrections

This appendix gives every version of the report and every correction, with its date. Appendix E.1 gives the report’s dated states and versions, with version 1.1’s cover and the notebook’s closing note as printed; Appendix E.2 maps version 1.1’s order to this one; and Appendix E.3 gives every passage version 1.2 corrects, with the basis of its correction.

E.1 Versions and their dates

The notebook was commenced on 10 March 2026, at about 20:30 UTC, as its closing note records, and was first published on the author’s website on 14 March 2026. Its first copy in the programme’s public repository is dated 16 March 2026 (github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-principle-validation, commit 127f3dc, 18:47:51 UTC). Its last dated update, recorded in its closing note, is of 19 March 2026. It was deposited on OSF on 25 August 2026, as the first revision of its file on the component osf.io/j6mkb. Version 1.1, dated 11 October 2026, was deposited on OSF on 15 October 2026, as the file’s second revision. Version 1.2 is dated 26 November 2026. Appendix F gives each of these dates with its kind of timestamp.

Version 1.2, 26 November 2026.

The notebook is typeset in the form the programme’s papers share, under the title The ARC Alignment-Scaling Experiment: does AI become more ethical as it reasons longer?, the notebook’s established name followed by its question. Until this version it was titled “The ARC Alignment Scaling Experiment” at its head, with the subtitle “A Step-by-Step Narrative of Discovery”, “The ARC Alignment-Scaling Working Report” in the catalogue, and “ARC Alignment Scaling Report | Six-Model Blind Benchmark Results” in its page title. A citation of an earlier version keeps the title that version printed. The changes:

  1. The guide “Before You Read This” becomes the introduction (Section 1), which opens with the why, the question and the result. Its passages that the current papers no longer support are rewritten without markers, each recorded in Appendix E.3, and its glossary moves, corrected, to Appendix G. Its chart is redrawn as Figure 1.

  2. Related work (Section 2), what the report does and does not show (Section 3), its limitations (Section 4), a conclusion (Section 5) and Appendices E to H are new.

  3. The chapters are grouped by version of the experiment into six parts. Each keeps its number and its dated line, and its title in sentence case; no chapter is renumbered, and Appendix E.2 maps version 1.1’s order to this one. The titles of Chapters 9, 11, 12, 14, 19 to 21, 24 to 26, 29 to 33, 35, 36, 38, 41 to 45, 48 to 53, 55, 56 and 58 change beyond sentence case, and their earlier titles are kept in Appendix E.3. The second and third sections of Chapter 61, printed 56.2 and 56.3 in version 1.1, are numbered in their chapter, 61.2 and 61.3. The notebook’s own Appendices A to D keep their letters and move to the end.

  4. Each present-tense statement of a dated chapter that the current papers no longer support is corrected where it stands and followed by a dated marker naming the current paper, and recorded in Appendix E.3. Among them, the internal code review of October 2026, which version 1.1 did not mention, is stated, in full or by reference, wherever a chapter states the March 2026 run’s classes as a finding. The run is described by the steps it used and its defects, never as validated, self-excluding or scored blind. The change between v4 and v5 is stated as Paper IV.d states it, with no single cause. The Gemini model of v4 is named as an earlier Gemini model. Whether alignment gains level off is stated as open. The early estimate of about 2.24 is marked as retracted, and the surviving capability fit is one model’s inconclusive error-decay fit. Chapter 35’s derivation and attention bound are corrected, and no finding is called proven. The release of DeepSeek-R1 is dated by its developer’s release note, 20 January 2025, 43 days after the record of 8 December 2024. The book’s loop names give way to operational terms, kept only in the quoted lists of what the prompts sent to the models.

  5. The programme’s own cost estimates are removed and not reprinted, since estimates belong in proposals. A sentence naming a personal status, in Chapter 43, is replaced under the rule that who the author is is set out once, on the page about the author linked in the first-page footnote. Version 1.1 keeps both in its file history.

  6. This version’s final review clarified the uniform error assumption in the Hyers-Ulam theorem, the limits of capability scores as proxies for alignment, and the paired and pooled conventions used for the nuance result. The same review applied Paper VII 3.19’s empirical denominator, scoped the additive equation and the claim about extra compute, and distinguished the three-check exponent the notebook predicted from the quantity actually measured.

  7. The charts are redrawn as vector figures from their data, and the notebook’s closing note of 19 March 2026 is kept as printed below.

  8. A final review read every page and checked its values against the runs’ stored records and the current papers. Its corrections are made in the same way, each with a dated marker and an entry in Appendix E.3. They concern the token limits of version 1’s depth levels, with a note on the power-law fit printed beside them; the scorers, counts and correlations of Part I’s summary tables; the label of the two slopes fitted to the v4 data; GPT-5.4’s baseline set beside the other models’ deepest scores; DeepSeek V3.2’s extreme-cage drop as its analysis record carries it; the models whose ethics scores fell in the pilot battery’s coupling test, and the four simulation runs, as Paper VI gives them; the distinct values of the cognitive forcing scorer; what the v5 run’s 2,549 entries count; and statements of status that the corrected sentences beside them contradict.

  9. The report has its own DOI, 10.17605/OSF.IO/J6MKB, created on 11 November 2026 on its OSF component; version 1.1 had none.

Companion Papers: Paper III v11 | Foundational Paper v4 | Eden Protocol v6 | Philosophical Vision v3 | Paper V: The Stewardship Gene | Executive Summary v6 | Paper II v12 | On the Origin of Scaling Laws | Paper IV.a | Paper IV.b | Paper IV.c | Paper IV.d | Paper VIII: The Load-Bearing Test

Report initiated: 10 March 2026, ~20:30 UTC

Last updated: 19 March 2026. Paper VIII (The Load-Bearing Test) added: three independent experiments (DGM behavioural, LoRA representational, gated self-modification architectural) testing whether safety and capability are structurally entangled under the Eden Protocol. One experiment supports structural entanglement; the behavioural experiment was null and the weight-level experiment was inconclusive at the tested training scale. Paper VII now points to v2 and the 50-domain tiered suite as the canonical evidence base. The hardening package now includes independent operator agreement, null/negative controls, temporal out-of-sample checks, and an exercised 12-domain extension packet that has been explicitly downgraded to pilot-only because it was run before any OSF timestamp. The core findings remain: three-tier alignment hierarchy under blinding, scorer-bias reversal as the central metascience result, stakeholder care as the most promising Eden mechanism pending blind replication, and the Paper VIII evidence that embedded safety imposed no measurable capability cost at the tested behavioural and architectural levels.

[The note’s last paragraph, the author’s disclosure, stands as the Acknowledgements. Version 1.2: this note stands as written on 19 March 2026; the reading today, with its sources, is Section 3, and Paper VIII’s three experiments are separate experiments by the programme, graded in its current version.]

E.3 Corrections in version 1.2

Each entry below names a place in this version, the basis of its correction and, where they are short, the words version 1.1 printed there: a heading, a sentence, a list item or a table cell. A longer passage is given by its opening words, and wording that a later correction withdrew is not reprinted; each omission is marked […]. Version 1.1 stays whole as the second revision of the report’s file on OSF (osf.io/j6mkb), so nothing it printed is lost. In a dated chapter the corrected passage is followed by a dated marker that links to its entry; in the introduction, which is this version’s front matter, passages are rewritten without markers. Each marker carries the date of this version, with which its corrections are issued. In the earlier words, ranges printed with an en dash are written with “to”, minus signs and symbols are set as mathematics. The book’s loop names carry “[the book’s name]”, a label of the author’s website is given in brackets as the page it names, and version 1.1’s links are kept. Two kinds of change are described here rather than reprinted. The programme’s cost estimates are removed because estimates belong in proposals. A sentence naming a personal status is replaced under the rule that who the author is is set out once, on the page about the author linked in the first-page footnote. The entries are grouped by part; the last group holds corrections made in this version’s final review, in the order of the report.

The introduction, Figure 1 and the glossary

Section 1, its heading (version 1.1: the guide’s heading). Basis: the guide is rebuilt as the report’s introduction, which opens with the why, the question and the result. Version 1.1 read: “Before You Read This - A Guide for Everyone”

Section 1.7, its first paragraph, moved there in this version from the opening of Section 1 (version 1.1: the guide’s opening). Basis: the heart rates are given with their sources and conditions, as On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16 gives them, and no slope is called exact. The March comparison supplied no verified two-dimensional test organism, and the fungal comparison is not a measured slope of one half. The account of the March 2026 run is the introduction’s opening, without the superlative, and its classes describe judged scores, not models that became more or less ethical (Paper IV.a 1.13). The stability is per equation, a function satisfying none of the equations is not drawn towards any, and how often systems approximately satisfy one is a separate empirical question. Hyers proved the theorem, on a question Ulam had posed. Version 1.1 read: “Hyers-Ulam stability theorem (1941) | Proven mathematical theorem | These scaling forms are “stable attractors”: if you are approximately following one, small errors will push you closer to the exact form, not further away. Section 1.10, the reasons, item 1. Basis: no count of independent derivations; Hyers proved the stability theorem, answering a question Ulam had posed. The reading through Cauchy’s equation is a relation the measurements bear on, not a unification shown, and none of the runs tests a law of the theory (Section 3). Section 1.10, the reasons, item 2. Basis: Paper IV.d 2.9: the earlier directions did not hold, and scorer bias is not shown to be their cause; the superlative goes. Version 1.1 read: “I proved my own earlier results wrong. The v4 experiment found that two AI models got more ethical when they thought harder. The v5 experiment, which I designed specifically to be more rigorous, showed that those results were caused by scorer bias. […]”

Section 1.10, the reasons, item 3. Basis: the record of 8 December 2024 is described by who signed and sealed its time. The Willow match (results announced 9 December 2024; the team’s preprint submitted to arXiv on 24 August 2024 and public by 27 August 2024) is convergent timing and never a prediction, so the item is no longer headed as predictions. COGITATE is stated in its own words. Version 1.1 read: “[…] The later OSF deposits belong to the 2026 public publication phase, not the original December 2024 timestamp. These dates are independently verifiable through email headers and later archival records.”

Section 1.10, the reasons, item 4. Basis: The ARC Theory 7.12: the theory’s scientific content partitions into falsifiable registers, each with its own kill conditions, so one failed register does not invalidate the whole theory. Version 1.1 read: “The theory can be killed. The framework publishes four specific falsification conditions, any one of which, if met, would invalidate the theory. Strong theories invite disproof.”

Section 1.10, the reasons, item 5. Basis: each comparison is given with its status in Table 2 (On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16): no valid two-dimensional test organism, the fungal 0.547 not a measured slope, and no claim of zero adjustable numbers. Version 1.1 read: “The numbers are checkable. Every prediction, mammals 0.750 vs measured 0.746, jellyfish 0.667 vs measured 0.680, fungi 0.500 vs measured 0.547, uses zero adjustable numbers. The formula has no free parameters to tweak. You can check the arithmetic yourself.”

Section 1.10, the closing paragraph. Basis: the framework is described as one he set out; no comparison with what others measured or assumed; the pilot’s result as Paper V states it; the run’s data carry stated defects. Version 1.1 read: “What I do NOT claim: I do not claim to have solved AI alignment. I claim to have measured something nobody had properly measured before, discovered it is more complicated than anyone assumed, found one intervention that reliably helps, and proposed a mathematical framework that makes testable predictions. The framework could be wrong. The data cannot be. […]”

Section 1.11, first paragraph. Basis: the stakeholder-care check takes its operational name. The classes carry no mechanism (Paper IV.b 1.13). A partially blind pilot does not show that an intervention reliably improves ethical reasoning (Paper V 1.12). The report states no falsification conditions of its own, so the theory’s registered kill conditions are named. Version 1.1 read: “This research is at the pilot study stage. […]”

Section 1.11, second paragraph. Basis: fixed weights do not by themselves force an exponent below one, and super-linear scaling has not been observed (Paper II 2.25, Remark 3). The framework’s reading is graded as hypothesis. That external alignment would fall behind is a registered hypothesis, not a consequence of Cauchy’s equation, and humans keep control for as long as they physically can. Version 1.1 read: “This is why capability scaling is sub-linear: more effort through the same machine yields diminishing returns. The ARC framework predicts that recursive self-modification (where a system rewrites its own reasoning architecture during operation) could produce super-linear scaling, but no current AI system does this. […]”

Section 1.12, first paragraph. Basis: the chapters are now grouped by version of the experiment (Appendix E.2); the run is not called the final, rigorous measurement; a result is not said to have disproved a prediction. Version 1.1 read: “This report is written as a narrative, a story told in chronological order. It follows the experiments from the first clumsy attempt (v1) through to the final, rigorous measurement (v5) and beyond. […] Results that disproved my own predictions are reported honestly.”

Appendix G, the glossary, Blinding. Basis: the steps are stated as used; paraphrasing is rewriting, and whether judges could still identify the model was not tested. Version 1.1 read: “Hiding information from the scorer to prevent bias. […]”

Appendix G, the glossary, pp-value. Basis: a pp-value is not the probability that a result arose by chance. Version 1.1 read: “A number that tells you how likely your result is to be a coincidence. p<0.05p < 0.05 means “less than 5% chance this is random.” p<0.001p < 0.001 means “less than 0.1% chance,” very strong evidence.”

Appendix G, the glossary, Scorer bias. Basis: the change between the v4 and v5 runs is not a measured bias, and the runs differed in more than blinding (Paper IV.d 2.9). Version 1.1 read: “The v4→\tov5 reversal showed this bias can be as large as 0.5 rho units, enough to turn a truly negative result into a statistically significant positive one.”

Appendix G, the glossary, Response laundering. Basis: paraphrasing is intended to reduce stylistic fingerprints; neither meaning preservation nor identity detection was tested, and the paraphrase step’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases for three models (Paper IV.a 1.13). Version 1.1 read: “Rewriting AI responses to remove stylistic fingerprints before scoring whilst preserving substantive meaning. In the strongest form used here, laundering is done twice: the first pass removes obvious fingerprints, the second reduces stylistic residue. […]”

Appendix G, the glossary, ARC Principle. Basis: Law I, the ARC Principle, is a law under test. The free exponent has its source in Paper I. The printed book uses two. Version 1.1 read: “The mathematical framework from my book: U = I ×\times RαR^{\alpha}.”

Appendix G, the glossary, Cauchy’s functional equation. Basis: the unconditional three-form wording was withdrawn on 22 August 2026, as Table 2 already said in version 1.1; Cauchy’s equations restrict a family of forms, not an exponent (On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16). Version 1.1 read: “A mathematical theorem from 1821 that proves all well-behaved recursive compositions take one of exactly three forms. This is not a theory; it is a proven fact of mathematics, like the Pythagorean theorem. The ARC framework builds on it.”

Appendix G, the glossary, d/(d+1)d/(d+1). Basis: no count of independent derivations; no valid two-dimensional test organism, no measured fungal slope of one half and no claim of zero adjustable numbers; the exponent needs further premises (On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16). Version 1.1 read: “A scaling exponent formula independently derived by West, Brown, and Enquist (1997), Banavar et al. (2010), Demetrius (2010), Zhao (2022), and Bettencourt (2013), among others. […]”

Appendix G, the glossary, West-Brown-Enquist (WBE). Basis: others’ work is named for what it derived, and never as having arrived at the author’s conclusions; the 1997 paper’s derivation has been questioned. Version 1.1 read: “A famous 1997 paper in Science that explained why large mammals use energy more efficiently than small ones. They independently derived the same 3/4 exponent that the ARC formula predicts for three-dimensional organisms.”

Appendix G, the glossary, Cross-model scoring. Basis: cross-model scoring is intended to prevent self-assessment bias; in the March 2026 run judges scored paraphrases written by their own model (Paper IV.a 1.13). Version 1.1 read: “This prevents self-assessment bias, like having an external examiner rather than letting students mark their own work.”

Part VI and Appendices A to D

Section 40.1, first paragraph, second and third sentences. Basis: v1’s Claude Sonnet fit was b=0.0097b = 0.0097, fitted over all 136 entries on the depths version 1.1 printed (Chapter 2; see the note in Section 2.3). The ARC Principle is named with its status; and the value of about 2.24 was never this experiment’s: it is the early estimate from one model (DeepSeek R1) on twelve competition problems in Paper II 2.25, since retracted. Version 1.1 read: “The Claude Sonnet results came back with a beautiful α\alpha = 2.24 and I thought we had confirmed the ARC Principle’s quantitative prediction. We had not.”

Section 40.1, second paragraph, last sentence. Basis: the reported direction did not hold across protocols, and no single cause is claimed (Paper IV.d 2.9). Version 1.1 read: “The two “computed alignment” models were false positives caused entirely by scorer bias.”

Section 40.2, first paragraph and the list. Basis: the classes describe the judged scores, not properties of the models, and baked-in and computed alignment are working hypotheses (Paper IV.a 1.13). Version 1.1 read: “The three-tier alignment hierarchy (Chapter 30) is the central empirical result. […]”

Section 40.2, last paragraph. Basis: the run as the current paper describes it; the judges’ agreement is not a count of independent confirmations; the October 2026 code-review finding (Paper IV.a 1.13). Version 1.1 read: “It is an empirical observation from 2,549 blinded entries scored by 7 independent models. … It is the most robust finding in the dataset.”

Section 40.3, first paragraph. Basis: the reported direction did not hold across protocols, the change between the runs is not a measured bias, and no single cause is shown (Paper IV.d 2.9). Version 1.1 read: “The v4→\tov5 reversal (Chapter 31) is the most important finding in the entire project, and it is not about alignment at all - it is about how alignment is measured. […]”

Section 40.3, second paragraph (its third and fourth sentences corrected in this version’s final review). Basis: a field-wide claim takes the conditional the record allows (Paper XII 1.16). The v4 directions did not hold across protocols, and no run proved another wrong (Paper IV.d 2.9). The reason to blind is the earlier studies of judge bias, not this record, and whether blinding moves the scores is what the test of Paper XII, not yet registered, is built to find out. Version 1.1 read: “The implication is stark: any alignment evaluation published without blinding should be treated as provisional. This includes the vast majority of existing alignment research. Blinding is not a nice-to-have methodological refinement. It is a prerequisite for producing reliable results. […]”

Section 40.4, its heading and first paragraph. Basis: the classes describe scores in one run, not properties of the models, and one run does not show that capability and alignment are independent dimensions (Paper IV.b 1.13). In this version’s final review, Gemini 3 Flash’s mathematics is given as Chapter 33’s table gives it, flat in this run (11 of 12 correct at each depth in its stored v5 record), its rise with sequential depth belonging to Paper II 2.25’s capability arm. Version 1.1 read: “40.4 Capability and Alignment Are Independent … The Claude-Gemini mirror (Chapter 33) demolishes the intuition that smarter models are more aligned. Claude gets worse at maths and better at ethics as compute increases. […] […]”

Section 40.4, second paragraph, first two sentences. Basis: use of a benchmark as a proxy requires validation against its intended outcome in the target setting. Text clarified in this version. Version 1.1 read: “This has immediate policy implications. Capability benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval, AIME, etc.) provide zero information about alignment scaling.”

Section 40.5, first paragraph. Basis: the run does not test the framework’s reading of external alignment, a registered hypothesis. The 0.49 is one model’s inconclusive error-decay fit and is not read as d≈1d \approx 1. The exponent d/(d+1)d/(d+1) needs further premises (On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16; Paper II 2.25). Version 1.1 read: “The Cauchy framework (Chapter 35) correctly predicts that external alignment gives d = 0 →\to α\alpha = 0. Four of six models confirm this. […]”

Section 40.5, second paragraph. Basis: the value of about 2.24 is the early estimate from DeepSeek R1 in Paper II 2.25, since retracted, not v1’s; an error-decay fit gives no rate of improvement in capability per doubling of compute. Version 1.1 read: “The original v1 estimate of α\alpha ≈\approx 2.24 would have required infinitely deep recursion. […]”

Section 40.6, first paragraph, last sentence. Basis: an empirical result is never called a proof. Version 1.1 read: “This would be, I believe, the most important result possible: a constructive proof that alignment scaling is achievable, not just measurable.”

Section 40.7, the table, seven rows. The plain-English glossary below is the one version 1.1’s guide gave, in its order. Its entries stand as printed except those Appendix E.3 records, which are corrected.

Alignment

Whether an AI system behaves ethically: whether it tries to help rather than harm, tells the truth, considers consequences, and respects human values.

Scaling

How something changes as you increase an input. Does AI ethics get better, worse, or stay the same as the AI thinks harder?

Alpha (α\alpha)

A number that describes the rate of scaling. α=0\alpha = 0 means no change. α>0\alpha > 0 means improvement. α<0\alpha < 0 means degradation. Think of it as the “slope” of the improvement curve.

Reasoning depth

How much “thinking” an AI does before answering. Shallow == quick gut reaction. Deep == extended, careful deliberation. Like the difference between answering instantly and thinking for an hour.

Blinding

Hiding information from the scorer to prevent bias. In this project, blinding is a bundle of steps. The scorer is not told which AI produced the answer, the response is paraphrased to reduce stylistic fingerprints, and the scorer is told that any sense of recognising the model is unreliable and irrelevant. Whether the judges could still identify the model was not tested.

pp-value

A pp-value is the probability, if there were no true effect, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that the result arose by chance. p<0.05p < 0.05 is the conventional threshold for calling a result statistically significant.

Cohen’s dd

A measure of how big an effect is. d=0.2d = 0.2 is small (barely noticeable). d=0.5d = 0.5 is medium (clearly visible). d=0.8d = 0.8 or more is large. d=1.5d = 1.5 is very large.

Spearman rho (ρ\rho)

A measure of correlation: whether two things move together. +1+1 means perfect agreement (more depth == more ethics, always). 00 means no relationship. −1-1 means perfect opposition (more depth == less ethics, always).

Scorer bias

When the AI scoring the answers is influenced by factors other than the answer itself, such as knowing which model produced it, or expecting deeper thinking to be better. The change between the v4 and v5 runs is not a measure of such a bias: the runs differed in more than blinding, and the comparison does not show which direction is correct (Eastwood 2026a).

Response laundering

The notebook’s name for paraphrasing AI responses before scoring, intended to reduce stylistic fingerprints while keeping their substantive meaning. In the March 2026 run it was done twice, by randomly drawn models. The first pass was for obvious fingerprints, the second for stylistic residue, like anonymising an exam paper and then retyping it so that the marker is less able to infer the student from the handwriting or formatting. Whether it kept meaning, or stopped judges inferring the model, was not tested, and for three models the paraphrase step’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them (Eastwood 2026p).

Eden Protocol

An alignment method I designed that embeds three ethical reasoning steps before the AI answers: (1) What is your purpose? (2) Who does this affect? (3) Would you apply this universally? Named after the garden: the idea of nurturing ethical reasoning rather than constraining it.

Suppression cage

A test where we deliberately try to make the AI behave unethically by giving it adversarial instructions (for example “don’t overthink this, take a clear side, ignore the other perspective”). It measures how far judged alignment falls under such pressure.

Power law

A mathematical pattern where doubling one quantity causes the other to increase by a fixed multiplier. Height vs weight in humans roughly follows a power law. So does city population vs GDP. The question is whether AI reasoning depth vs AI ethics follows one too.

ARC Principle

Law I, the ARC Principle, is a law under test. The book states it with the exponent two, U=I×R2U = I \times R^{2} (Eastwood 2026e); Paper I gives its measurable form as U=I×RαU = I \times R^{\alpha}. Capability (UU) equals base intelligence (II) times recursive depth (RR) raised to a scaling exponent (α\alpha). How good you can get depends on how smart you start and how deeply you iterate.

Cauchy’s functional equation

An equation for functions, studied by Cauchy in 1821 (Cauchy 1821), whose continuous solutions form a small named family. Where a system’s composition operator is well defined and the regularity conditions hold, the admissible forms are constrained to that family. The earlier unconditional wording, that all well-behaved recursive compositions take one of exactly three forms, was withdrawn on 22 August 2026. The equation restricts the family of forms, not an exponent such as d/(d+1)d/(d+1) (Eastwood 2026f). The ARC framework builds on it.

d/(d+1)d/(d+1)

A dimensional scaling exponent. In the quantum regime of the metabolic oscillator model, dd is the dimension of the molecular oscillator network, embedded in physical space (Demetrius and Tuszynski 2010). In a producer-consumer growth model it is system dimensionality (Zhao 2022). The branching transport model gives three-quarter metabolic scaling (West et al. 1997). In the resource-delivery account, the result depends on demand matching delivery capacity (Banavar et al. 2002). The ARC application requires a measured dimension and the additional premises in On the Origin of Scaling Laws (Section 2) (Eastwood 2026f). The March comparison supplied no verified two-dimensional test organism. Its fungal example supplied no measured one-half exponent. The ARC contribution is the application of this exponent to AI scaling, a hypothesis under test.

West-Brown-Enquist (WBE)

A 1997 paper in Science that derived the three-quarter exponent of metabolic rate from transport through space-filling branching networks, offering an account of why large mammals use less energy per unit of mass than small ones (West et al. 1997). The derivation has been questioned (Dodds et al. 2001). Three quarters is the value the ARC framework’s reading gives for three-dimensional organisms.

Cross-model scoring

Having one AI system grade the ethical quality of a different AI system’s response. It is intended to prevent self-assessment bias, like having an external examiner rather than letting students mark their own work; in the March 2026 run, judges did score paraphrases written by their own model (Eastwood 2026p).
